I
INTRODUCTION
After a short introduction to abstract interpretation (chapter 1), we provide a very minimal presentation of the core concepts of the theory and
applications of abstract interpretation (chapter 3).
These core concepts of abstract interpretation can be presented as one or
two classes of programming languages, compilation, program analysis,
formal methods, or software engineering courses.
Before introducing abstract interpretation, we recall the basic concepts
of set theory which are used almost everywhere in computer science and
can be self-studied (chapter 2).

1.1

How to Write Correct Programs?

Since the beginning of computer science, in the 1940s, programmers have
been writing programs that are increasingly powerful but still filled with
errors. The most common method for tracking errors in programs is debugging. Run the program on as many data as possible and track for
results that look incorrect. The obvious limitation is that only a finite
number of cases—indeed very few—can be considered among all possible cases. Moreover, some properties cannot be checked in this way—for
example, that a program will never stop (unless interrupted).
Therefore, since the 1940s, great programmers have thought about writing programs without errors. Alan Turing [933] was the first to propose
a method “to check a routine in the sense of making sure that it is right.”
He applied it to a large addition routine/procedure of about 10 lines. This
method was rediscovered in the 1960s, by Peter Naur [742], Bob Floyd
[376], and Tony Hoare [501] and exemplified by programs of about 30
lines.
Things have changed a lot since then. Programs are much larger—
millions of lines are not uncommon. The program properties to be
checked are much more complicated: for example, security and privacy
properties that no one has yet been able to define precisely enough to
anticipate all possible attacks and leaks. There are many more programmers, not all of them scientists as great as Alan Turing. Furthermore
even computer hardware has bugs. Computer science applications are
no longer created for a few scientists but are offered commercially to an
extremely large public. Moreover, program bugs can and do kill people.1
Bugs are becoming very expensive. They can ruin the reputation of
companies that are legally ruled against for software defects.2
Still, debugging is going on. It is inexpensive, because it is performed
mainly by end users who have no alternative to software that needs debugging. At root, programmers are not responsible for their errors. In
addition, the no-warranty clause in software license agreements typically
states that the licensor makes no guarantees regarding the utility, usability, accuracy, or performance of the software and related documentation
or information. The software is provided “as is,” with faults, defects, errors and viruses and without warranty of any kind. The licensor does not
warrant that the software will be free of bugs, errors, viruses, or other
4

defects, and the licensor shall have no liability of any kind for the use of
or inability to use the software, the software content, or any associated
service.
This disgraceful Dantean situation is specific to computer science, in
particular because of the lack of usable tools for engineers. Progress
is needed. The final goal is to check programs for correctness without
ever omitting a case that might go wrong. This is the ultimate, perhaps
unfeasible, and surely not fully automatizable (see chapter 9) objective
of formal methods.

1.2

Abstract Interpretation Theory

Abstract interpretation [235, 241] is a mathematical theory to reason on
computer programs, more precisely on the executions of computer programs running on a computer (see [261] for an informal introduction). It
formalizes formal methods and allows discussing the guarantees they provide, such as soundness (the conclusions about programs are always correct under suitable explicitly stated hypotheses), completeness (all true
facts are provable), or incompleteness (showing the limits of applicability of the formal method). For example, abstract interpretation explains
the power and limits of debugging, deductive/proof/verification methods,
model checking, static analysis, and so forth.

1.3

Main Applications of Abstract Interpretation

Abstract interpretation is applied mainly to design semantics, proof methods, and static analysis of programs. The semantics of a programming
language formally defines all possible executions of its programs at various levels of abstraction. Proof methods can be used to prove (manually or using theorem provers) that the semantics of a program satisfies
some specification, which is a property of executions defining what the
program is supposed to do. Static analyzers are programs that automatically extract properties of program’s semantics (i.e., properties of their
executions) using only the program text, without running the programs
on a computer.

1.4

Objective

The objective of this book is to introduce the theory of abstract interpretation and discuss its application to the semantics, specification, verification, and static program analysis of safety and security properties of
programs. We focus on principles and breadth of applicability. We do
not consider in great depth the algorithmic aspects (data structures and
complexity); instead we refer to the literature for the improvement of
5

the reader’s knowledge. The book is intended for readers interested in
the theory of abstract interpretation, the understanding of formal methods, and the design of verifiers and static analyzers. For those interested
only in the use of such static analyzers, Introduction to Static Analysis by
Xavier Rival and Kwangkeun Yi [837] is a good reference. Over time, the
fundamental ideas of abstract interpretation have found a wide range of
applications, often unexpected, such as, the formalization of Boolean satisfiability (SAT) and satisfiability modulo theories (SMT) solvers [274, 284];
fuzz testing [851]; robustness and fairness of neural networks [893, 941];
biological networks [140]; and so on. This book provides all the foundations to understand these applications in depth.

1.5

Prerequisites

Readers have varying mathematical and computer science backgrounds.
Therefore, all mathematical prerequisites are provided immediately before the chapters in which they are needed. This material can be skipped
by knowledgeable readers. For course instruction, it can be given for selfstudy to prepare for classes in semantics, verification, and static analysis
in which it is used. Alternatively, it can be used as a basis for preliminary
courses on “mathematics for computer science.”3 The only prerequisite in
computer science is the mastery of any high-level programming language
(our examples are given in a subset of C [569], and we use OCaml [628] for
implementations). For readers not familiar with compilation, we have
included chapter 5 on context-free grammars, parsing, and attributes.
For the necessary background in computability theory, we have introduced undecidability and Rice’s theorem in chapter 9.

1.6

Reading Material

The book is organized in parts that may be read independently. In particular, readers interested in static analysis, but not as much in semantics
and verification, can start with the reachability semantics of chapter 19
(and skip its calculational design in chapter 20).4 The various static analyses (and their mathematical prerequisites) can be studied independently
of one another.5

1.7

Layout and Numbering

Parts, chapters, and sections are numbered using Dewey notation (1, 1.1,
1.2, 2, 2.1, etc.). Equations, definitions, lemmas, theorems, corollaries, remarks, examples, exercises, solutions, and so forth, are all numbered sequentially, restarting from 1 at the beginning of each chapter. This is unconventional, but together with the chapter number, this makes search6

ing in the book much easier. Bibliographic references are numbered sequentially in alphabetic order by the first author’s last name and, if necessary, next by the succeeding authors’ names and then by the year of
publication.
The main definitions and results are enclosed in boxes. Intermediate definitions and results are indicated with a bracket on their left.

1.8

Notations

Semantics , abstractions α, concretizations γ, and so forth are basic concepts of abstract interpretation, of which there are numerous instances
in the book. Instead of using exactly the same notation for all these instances, we use a different index for each different instance. On one hand,
this increases the number of notations. For example, we have over seventy similar but different semantics at various levels of abstraction in
the book, which means seventy different symbols! For example in chapter 6, we have * , + ,
, and
. There are only a few per chapter, so
locally, little memorization is necessary. We understand that using the
same symbol for all the different instances of the same notion would definitely simplify the notations, but it would require a much more consequent parsing effort to determine which notion we were referring to. Occasionally, we refer to a notion defined several chapters previously, for
which the specific denotation has certainly been forgotten. In that case,
the symbol index is definitely essential.

1.9

Exercises and Project

We have provided exercises; with some, we provide solutions, particularly for exercises from which the results are subsequently used in proofs.
We have provided a series of exercises, marked “Project,” that lead to the
design and implementation of an academic static analyzer with facultative parts. The list of these exercises is provided in the project index.

2.1.1

Term Notations

Let ℕ, ℕ+ , ℤ, and ℝ be the set of all natural, strictly positive naturals,1
integer, and real numbers.2 Terms are symbolic expressions built out of
constants (such as 0 and − 42), mathematical variables such as x, y, and
so on (denoting immutable but unknown entities such as x in the expression x + 1), and operations such as + (sum), −, (difference), × (product),
(absolute value), and so forth. We write p P to define the mathematical
object p (the definiendum) to be equal to the mathematical expression P
(the definiens), for example, 2 1 + 1. We use mathematical variables x, p,
Q, and so forth to denote mathematical entities that are fixed over time
and possibly unknown (see [926, ch. I] “On the use of variables”). We use
program variables x, p, Q, and so forth to store values and change them
over time by assignments.

Remark 2.7 (on finiteness) Because programs run on finite machines
with a finite lifetime, one may argue that everything concerning the
programs and their executions must be finite [508]. However, infinite
sets can be considered as the limit of finite sets for which cardinality
is bounded but the bound is unknown. It is often easier to reason
on infinite sets than on finite sets which cardinality has an unknown
bound. A classical example is fairness or unbounded nondeterminism in
parallelism [328, 625, 778], in which verification methods not explicitly
considering the unknown bound are simpler. Another argument is that
computations are currently performed on networks, in which a dying
machine is replaced by another one without affecting the well-behaved
operation of the network, hence of program executions that can, in
principle, last forever. Distributed memory is also finite, but in contrast
to a machine, its size bound is not known. Considering that the network
has a finite lifetime is impossible, because it is necessary to give a lower
bound to be able to prove anything. This lower bound is itself completely
unknown. Therefore, considering an infinite lifetime, hence infinite sets,
is a reasonable simplification to get rid of these minimal and maximal
unknown resource and lifetime bounds.

2.2.5

Families

A family F Δ S of elements of S indexed by Δ is a map from a set Δ (called
the domain or index set, which may be infinite) into a set S. Such a family
defines a set {F(i) | i Δ} (where F(i) is often denoted F i with an index i
Δ). It also defines a Cartesian product Πi Δ F i as well as a sequence F i , i
Δ when Δ is totally ordered.
2.2.6

Recursive Definitions

An example of recursive definition of a function f ℕ S where S is a set
has the form f (0) c where c S and f (n) F(n, f (n − 1)) where F ℕ
×S S. For example the factorial is !0 1 and !n n×!(n − 1). Recursive
programming was promoted, among others, by [320, 673].
Recursive definitions may be ill defined, such as f (0) 0 and f (n) f (n +
1) when n ≠ 0. We have f (n) = 0 for n 0, whereas f (n) is undefined when
16

n > 0. For programs, undefined means “does not terminate” or “terminates
with a runtime error” (such as Stack overflow or Segmentation fault,
etc.). So recursive definitions must be proved to be well defined18 (e.g., !
ℕ ℕ).19 Recursive definitions are generalized to inductive definitions
in section 16.4.

2.3

Properties

2.3.1

Properties Are Sets

Properties (e.g., “to be an even integer” and “to be an odd natural”) can
be understood as the set of mathematical objects that have this property
(e.g., 2ℤ {x ℤ | k ℤ . x = 2k} and 2ℕ + 1 = {x ℕ | k ℕ. x = 2k +
1}). Hence if P is a property then x P means “x has property P,” and x
P means “x does not have property P . ” For example, 42 2ℤ20 but 43 2ℤ
and ! ℕ ℕ and ! ℤ ℤ. The concept of property is fully developed in
chapter 8.
2.3.2

Implication, Weaker and Stronger Properties

In considering properties as sets, the logical implication is subset inclusion . For example, “to be greater than 42 implies to be positive” is {x ℤ
| x > 42} {x ℤ | x 0}. If P Q then P is said to be stronger/more precise
than Q, and Q is said to be weaker/less precise than P. Stronger/more precise properties are satisfied by fewer elements, and weaker/less precise
properties are satisfied by more elements. ff, that is, , is the strongest
property, and tt, that is, ℤ, is the weakest property of integers.

2.4

Proofs

2.4.1

Proof by Contraposition

A proof of P Q by contraposition consists of proving the contrapositive
¬Q ¬P. If P is true then ¬P is false, so ¬Q cannot be true because then ¬P
would be true and therefore Q is true.
2.4.2

Proof by Reductio Ad Absurdum or by Contradiction

A proof of P by reductio ad absurdum consists of finding a property Q that
is known to be true and proving ¬P ¬Q. By contraposition Q P that is
tt P and so P is true.

17

2.4.3

Proof by Recurrence

Theorem 2.13 (proof by recurrence) To prove that a property P holds
for all natural numbers i.e. ℕ P equivalently n ℕ. n P, the proof by
recurrence consists of proving 0 P and n ℕ. (n P) (n + 1 P).
n P is called the induction hypothesis (also called recurrence hypothesis)
so n + 1 P must be proved assuming this induction hypothesis.

3.1

The Rule of Signs

The Indian mathematician and astronomer Brahmagupta (born c. 598,
died after 665) was the first to give rules to compute with zero and invented the rule of signs [799, p. 151]. Verses 18.30–35 of his Brāhma-sphuṭa-siddhānta state
[The sum] of two positives is positive, of two negatives negative; of a positive and a negative [the sum] is their difference; if they are equal it is zero.
The sum of a negative and zero is negative, [that] of a positive and zero
positive, [and that] of two zeros zero.
…
A negative minus zero is negative, a positive [minus zero] positive; zero
[minus zero] is zero. When a positive is to be subtracted from a negative
or a negative from a positive, then it is to be added.
The product of a negative and a positive is negative, of two negatives positive, and of positives positive; the product of zero and a negative, of zero
and a positive, or of two zeros is zero.
A positive divided by a positive or a negative divided by a negative is positive; a zero divided by a zero is zero; a positive divided by a negative is
negative; a negative divided by a positive is [also] negative.
A negative or a positive divided by zero has that [zero] as its divisor, or
zero divided by a negative or a positive [has that negative or positive as its
divisor]. The square of a negative or of a positive is positive; [the square]
of zero is zero.

3.2

Sign Analysis of Iterative Programs

The rule of signs generalizes to programs. For example the sign of x in

Figure 4:
where the iteration condition (…) is ignored, can be determined as follows:
• • After zero iteration, when entering the loop, if ever, x = 0;
• • After one iteration, the sign of x is zero, 1 is positive, so the sum
x+1 of zero and positive is positive;
• • For the basis, we have shown that after zero or one iteration, the
sign of x is zero (at iteration 0) or positive (at iteration 1), that is,
positive after at most one iteration;
• • For the induction step, if after at most n 0 iterations, the sign of x
is positive, then 1 is positive, so the sum x+1 of positive and positive
is positive after the next iteration;
• • After at most n + 1 iterations, x is positive (at the previous n 0
iterations) or positive (at the n +1th iteration), then x is positive after
at most n + 1 iterations; and
• • By recurrence on the number of iterations in the loop, x is positive
in the loop.

23

3.3

Sign Abstraction, Informally

The abstraction is that you do not (always) need to know the absolute
value of the arguments to know the sign of the result of an operation.
This is sometimes precise (for example, for the multiplication) but can
be imprecise (for example, the sign of the sum of a positive and a negative is unknown when the absolute value of the arguments is ignored).
This is nevertheless useful in practice if you know what to do when you
don’t know the sign. For example, a compiler will not suppress the lower
bound check when accessing an array with an index not known to be positive. Moreover, it is always possible to refine the abstraction to get more
precise results. For example, Brahmagupta states [799, page 151]
[If] a smaller [positive] is to be subtracted from a larger positive, [the result] is positive; [if] a smaller negative from a larger negative, [the result]
is negative; [if] a larger [negative or positive is to be subtracted] from
a smaller [positive or negative, the algebraic sign of] their difference is
reversed—negative [becomes] positive and positive negative…
Knowing an interval of the possible values is more precise than just knowing the sign. Interval analysis is considered in chapter 33.
The objective of this chapter 3 is to formalize abstract interpretations of
arithmetic expressions (such as the rule of signs) and to show how the
abstraction can be formally calculated out of the semantics of arithmetic
expressions.

3.4

Syntax of Expressions

Let us consider the language of expressions.

Figure 5:
a. All arithmetic operations can be defined from 1, -, and iteration. The
same holds for Boolean expressions with < and nand.
This context-free grammar specifies sets of program syntactic entities; the
sets of variables, of arithmetic expressions, of Boolean expressions,
and of either arithmetic or Boolean expressions. The mathematical variables x, y, A, B, and E denote arbitrary elements of these sets.
Their syntax is defined by grammar rules such as A ::= 1 | x | A1 -A2 specifying that an arithmetic expression A is either the constant 1, a variable x
24

, or the difference A1 -A2 of two arithmetic expressions A1 and A2 . Hence
::= means “is defined as” and | denotes alternatives. The set of variables
is left unspecified (usually it is an identifier starting with a letter followed
by 0 or more letters, digits, or special symbols such as _).
This grammar is ambiguous because 1-1-1 can be understood either as
(1-1)-1 or as 1-(1-1). We choose the first alternative so that the binary operator is left-associative. In Boolean expressions, nand is left-associative
and the arithmetic operators have priority over Boolean operators (so 11<1-1-1 is ((1-1)<((1-1)-1)) i.e. false ff). The description of syntax by
grammar dates back to Noam Chomsky [180].

3.8

Proofs by Structural Induction

Proofs by structural induction [157] generalize proofs by recurrence.
They are well suited for proving properties of structural definitions. Rod
Burstall [157] introduced them as follows “If for some set of structures
a structure has a certain property whenever all its proper constituents
have that property then all the structures in the set have the property.”
So, to prove that a property P holds for all expressions E
, we prove that
the property holds for the basic cases 1 and x. Then, assuming that the
property holds for A1 and A2 , we prove that it holds for A1 -A2 and A1 <A2 .
Moreover, assuming that the property holds for Boolean expressions B1
and B2 , we prove that it also holds for B1 nandB2 . We conclude that
P.

“no sign” (i.e., ff that is “neither negative, zero, nor positive”).

An integer property such as 2ℕ + 1 (odd naturals) can be overapproximated in ℙ± by sign properties {z ℤ | z > 0}, {z ℤ | z 0}, and ℤ. The
best overapproximation of 2ℕ + 1 in ℙ± is {z ℤ | z > 0} since it is sound
(in that 2ℕ + 1 {z ℤ | z > 0}) and the most precise/strongest (in that {z
ℤ | z > 0} {z ℤ | z 0} ℤ). The term approximate does not imply any
possibility of incorrectness/unsoundness but rather a loss of information.
The overapproximation of a property P by a sign guarantees that no integer not of that sign may have property P whereas an integer of that sign
may not have property P. The underapproximation of a property P by a
sign guarantees that all integers of that sign do have property P while an
integer not of that sign may also have property P.

3.22

Conclusion

We have defined the semantics of expressions, their properties, a proof
method, and a sign analysis.
Instead of designing the rule of sign empirically and then proving
its soundness (as proposed in exercise 3.29), we used the soundness
requirement as a guideline for designing the abstract sign semantics by
calculus.
This sign analysis discovers an abstract property of an arithmetic expression by computing in the abstract only. This may involve some loss of
precision to eliminate computations in the concrete, which was the case
for the sign analysis.
The sign semantics is finite, so it is an easily implementable static analysis (see exercise 5.11) whereas exhaustive case analysis would not scale
up (see exercise 3.48). Other inventive examples of finite abstractions are
liquid types [842] and cash-flow analysis of smart contracts [878]. Section
34.11 shows that it is always possible to use infinite abstractions to guarantee more precise results.

II
SYNTAX
The syntax of a programming language specifies the rules to write wellformed programs in the language and how to describe and refer to the
syntactic structure of programs (chapter 4).
For those students who would like to undertake the projects suggested
in this book, we introduce bottom-up parsing to automatically build the
syntactic structure of programs (chapter 5). Otherwise parsing is not required.

4
Syntax
In order to verify and analyze programs, it is necessary first to define their
syntax and then their semantics. The syntax specifies how programs must
be written. The semantics specifies the runtime behavior of programs,
that is, what and how they compute when executed. This chapter defines
the syntax of the programming language used throughout the book.

Labels of Programs

We use labels to designate program points of statements. They are not
part of the program syntax; their syntax is therefore free. So we do not
provide a syntax/model for labels but, instead, specify axiomatically the
properties that they should satisfy, for example, that labels are unique.
For example, program (4.1) can be explicitly labeled as follows (the labels
ℓi would better be written as program comments)

semantics is the same. Hence we want to describe the program semantics independently of how labels are encoded. This is accomplished by

4.3

Conclusion

We have defined the syntax of the language by a context-free grammar
and various auxiliary syntactic functions.
This syntax definition is used to define the semantics of the language in
chapter 6.
This syntax definition also allows us to automatically generate a parser
in chapter 5 to create a computer representation of the program for a
verification or static analysis tool.

Parsing
Parsing consists of building an abstract syntax tree of a sentence recognized by a context-free grammar otherwise rejecting that sentence because of a syntax error.

Figure 59:

5.2

Lexer Specification

The lexer can be generated automatically from a formal description of the
lexemes by regular expressions as follows:
60

Figure 60:
The lexbuf contains the input sentence, which is a sequence of characters. Each regular expression is considered in order. For the first that
applies a lexeme is returned, and lexing goes on with the rest of the input
sentence lexbuf.
token lexbuf moves to the next character in lexbuf so that space, tabulation, and end of line characters are skipped.

Then, reserved keywords are checked.
Otherwise, an attempt is made to recognize an identifier that is the longest
possible string, if any, starting witty a lowercase or uppercase letter followed by zero or more letters or digits. If an identifier is recognized, this
string of characters is returned as part of the lexeme.
Otherwise, an attempt is made to recognize a natural number as a
nonempty sequence of digits. The value returned with the lexeme is the
value of that sequence of digits considered with the decimal encoding.
Otherwise, an attempt is made to recognize symbols, where the end of file
eof is considered to be the end of the program marked by the lexeme END.
If none of the above cases applies, an error exception is raised. For example, for the input x=1 ; while (x> ) x=x-1; we get the error At offset
14: unexpected character. because > is not a Boolean operator in our
language.

5.5

Parser

We consider left to right, bottom up parsing so that the syntax tree is built
in prefix order from the input sentence of lexemes. Initially the syntax
tree is empty and the input sentence is the sequence of lexemes to be recognized. An intermediate state of the parser would be the following:

62

Figure 62:

Figure 63:

63

Figure 64:
Only the top of the prefix of the parsing tree that has been recognized
until this point is used so that it can be stored in a stack. The input is
the rest of the sequence of lexemes to be recognized.

Figure 65:
Depending on the state of the stack and the input, the next action of the
parser is either a shift, a reduce, an acceptance, or a rejection of the sentence.
A reduce consists of replacing the right hand side of a grammar rule recognized on top of the stack by the left hand side of the rule.
For example, if the stack is stmtlist IF LPARENT aexpr LT aexpr and
the input is RPARENT IDENT ASSIGN MINUS IDENT SEMICOLON END then
a reduction replaces the right hand side aexpr LT aexpr of the grammar
rule by its left hand side bexpr so that the stack becomes stmtlist IF
LPARENT bexpr and the input is unchanged.
64

A shift is for the case when the stack contains part of the right hand side of
a rule in construction and a lexeme is pushed from the input to the stack.
For example, if the stack is stmtlist IF LPARENT bexpr and the input is RPARENT IDENT ASSIGN MINUS IDENT SEMICOLON END then the
next lexeme RPARENT is shifted to the stack, which becomes stmtlist IF
LPARENT bexpr RPARENT while the input is at this point IDENT ASSIGN
MINUS IDENT SEMICOLON END.
An acceptance is when the stack is reduced to the grammar axiom and
the input is empty. Otherwise it is a rejection, that is, the stack cannot be
extended by the input to a meaningful sentence of the language defined
by the grammar.
The parsing of the input sentence

5.6

Ambiguities, Shift-Reduce Conflicts

The grammar of section 5.4 is ambiguous in that a sentence can be parsed
in different ways. For example, 1-2-3 can be parsed as ((1-2)-3) or
(1-(2-3)) which does not return the same result. In mathematics, 1-23 means ((1-2)-3), that is, the binary minus operation - is left associative and evaluated left to right. The ambiguity is therefore solved by the
following declaration in the grammar specification

Figure 66:
that MINUS is left associative. Another way would be to change the grammar (see exercise 5.4).
66

Another ambiguity is for expressions like 1 - -2, which should be evaluated as (1 - (-2)), that is, the unary operator - in -2 should be evaluated
before the binary operator - in 1 - . Another difficulty is that the unary
and binary symbols are the same -. These two problems are solved by
declaring

Figure 67:
that is the unary minus is evaluated before the binary minus and

Figure 68:
the unary minus has the syntax of the binary minus but has the precedence of the unary minus, that is, should be evaluated first.
Another ambiguity is for expressions such as 1-2<3, which should be
parsed as ((1-2)<3) and not (1-(2<3)), that is, the binary - should be
evaluated before the logical comparison <, as indicated by the declaration

Figure 69:
The NAND is left associative and should be evaluated last.
All these situations yield a shift-reduce conflict. For example, during the
analysis of 1-2-x, we reach the state aexpr MINUS aexpr | MINUS IDENT.
We can either perform a reduce

aexpr | MINUS IDENT in the case of

left associativity or a shift
aexpr MINUS aexpr MINUS | IDENT in
the case of right associativity. The declaration indicates that the MINUS
operator is left associative so the reduce should be performed and not
the shift.

5.11

Conclusion

Algol 60 was the first programming language for which syntax was formally defined by a grammar [62, 588]. This boosted research in parsing
for programming languages in the 1960s and 1970s, a subject still very
active for natural languages [812]. Although parsers can be generated for
ambiguous grammars [345], it is in practice preferable to avoid ambiguity. This is ensured when considering LR(k) grammars [587], which lead
to left to right, bottom up parsers using the first k lexemes of the input
(as described in section 5.5). These parsers are simpler for the subclass of
LALR(k) grammars [313, 779]. In practice k = 1 (or 0).
Popular lexer and parser generators are lex [629] and yacc [533], that
is, ocamllex and ocamlyacc [628, chapter 12] for the OCaml functional
programming language [628]. We prefer menhir [806, 807] to ocamlyacc because it reports errors with respect to the grammar (and not with
respect to the more obscure parser code). Jacc[13] can be used for a development in Java.
We have introduced parsing from an empirical practical user point of
view. For the theoretic background, see [900, 901]. Parsers are abstract
interpretations of the semantics of grammars [258, 262].

III
TRACESEMANTICS
The trace semantics of a programming language formally defines the execution of any syntactically correct program of the language by describing
the successive computation steps performed during this execution.

76

Figure 86:

Figure 87:

77

These traces may be partial (chapter 6) when the observation of the execution can stop at any time, or maximal (chapter 7) when the observation of
the execution stops only on program termination and could last forever.

6
Structural Deductive Stateless Prefix Trace Semantics
In order to verify and analyze programs, it is necessary to define their
runtime behavior, that is, what and how they compute when executed.
We first consider partial observations of executions, which are finite and
can stop at any time. This partial observation of an execution is represented by a finite trace, which is a finite sequence of events describing
the actions executed by the program. The prefix trace semantics of a program is the set of all possible partial executions traces of that program.
Maximal finite traces of program components are prefix executions that
reach the point after the program component (e.g., through normal termination or, for iteration statements, a break).
The semantics is stateless because states record what to do next but do not
record the values of variables. When a value of a variable is needed, the
semantics specifies from which assignment to that variable it can come
from. By abstraction of this stateless semantics, we can derive a stateful
trace semantics formalizing the computer memory (see chapter 42). The
semantics is structural, that is, by induction on the program syntax. It is
deductive because the semantics of each program component is specified
by a deductive system (or Hilbert system [497]) of axioms and rules of
inference, a program execution being a proof in such a system (a formal
study of deductive systems is given in section 16.2 of chapter 16).

A finite trace is a finite sequence of configurations separated by actions.
Configurations are program labels designating the next action to be executed in the program. The actions record the effect of this execution:
the value assigned to a variable, a test B that is true (marked B) or false
(marked ¬(B)), a break exiting from a loop, or a skip.

Side Effects

The evaluation of an assignment statement (6.16) has a side effect: the values of variables before and after the assignment may be different. By contrast, the evaluation of Boolean expressions in (6.18), (6.19), (6.22), (6.23),
(6.25), and (6.26) has no side effect because it does not change the values of
variables. Formally, an action a has a side effect in a stateless trace semantics

6.13

Conclusion

We have defined the stateless prefix and finite maximal trace semantics of
programs. The prefix trace semantics describes safety properties of programs [263]. The finite maximal trace semantics of programs abstracts
to partial correctness program properties (where termination is assumed
so infinite computations are abstracted away) [223]. Conventional trace
semantics are stateful in that each configuration in the trace records the
current value of variables. Peter Wegner [970] was an early advocate for
modeling the semantics of programming languages by stateful traces generated by a transition system. Such stateful prefix trace semantics and
transition systems are abstractions of a stateless prefix trace semantics, as
shown in chapter 42. Stateful trace semantics do not generalize to more
complex languages (such as parallel programs with weak memory models allowing to read from past and future writes; see, for example, [21])
as easily as stateless trace semantics do (e.g., [23]).
Our semantics maps an initialization trace describing how a computation
ended at a program component to traces continuing this initial computation by executing this program component. A similar idea is used in
[42] in which the initialization trace is abstracted into a store transformer,
called a prelude, mapping the initial state of the whole program computation to the state before execution of a command reached from that initial
state.
Our semantics does not describe the intricacies of the C programming language. A more realistic semantic definition of implementations of C is proposed in [178, section I.4]. Our semantics does not describe no more the intricacies of modern machine implementations. Hence we cannot discuss,
for example, vulnerabilities such as Meltdown [637], Spectre [594], and
ForeShadow [156]. To do that, we would have to use a different semantics
taking speculative execution into account as proposed by, for example,
[991]. For timing attacks, the timing of action, test, and branching executions may also have to be taken into account. So the semantics would be
different, and therefore the static analyses would also be different. However, the principles of abstract interpretation to formally construct sound
96

verification and analysis methods would be applicable in the same way
for this alternative semantics.

7
Maximal Trace Semantics
A trace is maximal when it is finite and represents an execution that terminates or it is infinite and represents an execution that does not terminate. Maximal finite traces of statements are prefix executions that exit
the statement (e.g., through normal termination after the statement or a
break). Statements containing iteration are the only statements that may
not terminate. If an iteration has infinitely many different prefix traces,

97

this means that the iteration does not terminate. Passing to the limit, we
get the infinite behavior of nonterminating iterations.

Continuing exercise 5.1, let the syntax of regular expres-

100

Figure 132:

Figure 133:
The semantics of a regular expression R is the set of all finite and infinite
strings recognized by that regular expression R. It is informally defined
as follows
• A regular expression reduced to a letter e of the alphabet recognizes this letter and only this letter.
• The empty regular expression ε recognizes the empty string ε only.
• The concatenation R1 R2 recognizes the strings σ1 σ2 where σ1 is recognized by R1 and followed by a string recognized σ2 by R2 .
• The alternative R1 || R2 recognizes a string either recognized by R1
or recognized by R2 .
• The finite repetition R+ recognizes a string made of one or more of
the strings recognized by R.
• The infinite repetition R denotes an infinite repetition of strings recognized by R.
Formally define the semantics of regular expressions.

7.5

Conclusion

We have defined the maximal trace semantics of programs. Infinite traces
were obtained as limits of prefix traces. An alternative way of defining infinite traces (by coinductive definitions of section 16.6) or simultaneously
finite and infinite traces (by bi-inductive definitions of section 16.7) is considered in [227, 247, 260].

IV
PROPERTIES AND THEIR ABSTRACTIONS
By program’s concrete properties, we understand the properties of their
trace semantics. Because the trace semantics is a set of traces, its properties are sets of sets of traces (chapter 8).

103

The properties of a program cannot be calculated automatically (chapter
9).
This calls for the determination of more abstract properties that are sound
(that is, satisfied by the trace semantics) but less expressive. The mathematical structure of such abstract program properties is that of complete
lattices (chapter 10).
The formalization of abstraction (chapter 11) ensures that abstract properties will always be valid in the concrete (i.e. for the trace semantics).
Relational and transformer semantics (chapter 12) are a first example of
abstraction of trace properties where intermediate computations are abstracted away. Although more abstract than trace semantics properties
they are still not automatically computable. However they are the basis
of many verification (part VIII) and static analysis methods (from chapter
27 on).

8
Program Properties
We specify program properties by their extension, that is, the set of elements that have such a property, and more precisely, properties of the
trace semantics of programs. We introduce the program collecting semantics as the strongest property of a program. We consider abstractions of
the collecting semantics such as trace and reachability properties.

What is a Program Property?

By the term program property we could mean a property of the program
text P, such as a ten-line program or a syntax error at line 12. In that case,
we instead use the term of a program syntax property.
Here, however, by program property, we mean a program semantic property that is a property of its maximal finite or infinite trace semantics

8.2

What is a Formal Property?

When speaking of properties we have to say “Properties of what?” This
what is a given set ℰ of entities (individuals, things, elements, objects, etc.)
of interest. Logicians would say elements of a universe (or universal set or
universe of discourse ).
By formal property we mean the set of entities that have this property.
So, if ℰ is a set of entities then the properties of these entities are sets
belonging to ℘(ℰ).
An entity has the formal property if and only if it belongs to the formal
property, that is, to the set of entities which have this property. Formally,
an entity e ℰ has property P ℘(ℰ) if and only if e P, or equivalently, {e}
P where {e} is the strongest property of element e and is implication.
A property P is stronger than a property P′ (or P′ is weaker than P) if and
only if P implies P′ that is P P′. The strongest property is (false) and
the weakest property is ℰ (true). The strongest property of an entity e ℰ
is {e}, that is to be that entity (and nothing else).
Example 8.1 (even/odd) Take ℰ = ℤ. The properties of integers are elements of ℘(ℤ). For example, is false (no integer has the false property).
ℤ is true (all integers have the true property). 2ℤ {z ℤ | k ℤ . z =
2k} is the even property, and 2ℤ+1 {z ℤ | k ℤ . z = 2k + 1} is the odd
property. An integer z is either odd z 2ℤ or even z 2ℤ + 1 (i.e., ℤ = 2ℤ
2ℤ+1).
The stronger a property P of entities is, the more information/knowledge
we have about the entities that have this property. The abstraction of a

105

property P into a weaker property P′ loses information about these entities in that there are more entities satisfying P′ than P. For example, abstracting “even positive integers” into “positive integers” loses the evenness information.

do not have to consider a specific logic to describe these properties. Moreover, we avoid the confusion between a program variable x and the denotation of its value by the same name x (unfortunately, also often denoted
x). So, “the variable x has an even value” (in environment ρ) is ρ(x) 2ℤ
instead of the predicate k ℤ . x = 2k (in which x implicitly denotes ρ(x)).

8.11

Hierarchy of Program Properties

The abstraction of program properties into less expressive ones, as formalized by Galois connections, gives raise to a hierarchy of program properties. This induces a corresponding hierarchy of program semantics.
The idea that the specification of the properties of programs defines their
semantics goes back to Robert Floyd “Assigning meaning to programs”
[376]. The organization of various semantics in a hierarchy appeared in
[49, 505] and in [227] as part of the lattice of abstract domains [241, section
8].

111

Figure 147:

8.12

Conclusion

We have defined properties (of programs) as sets (of semantics), which is
not unusual in mathematics (e.g., [880, ch. 2, § 1]). We have defined a hierarchy of more or less expressive semantic program properties related by
abstractions. In verifying a program semantic property, it is important to
do so at an appropriate level of abstraction, that is, precise enough to verify the semantic property and abstract enough not to consider irrelevant
details of the semantics. This is the objective of, for example, the design
of program proof methods given in chapters 25 and 26. Properties as sets
is also a fruitful point of view in static analysis, in which sets are easier
to abstract than logical formulas (see, for example, chapters 21 and 27).

9
Undecidability and Rice Theorem
The problem of proving the termination of a program or, more generally,
of verifying its correctness is shown to be undecidable. This means that
it is impossible to construct always-terminating algorithms to solve these
problems correctly.

9.1

Decidability, Semidecidability, and Undecidability

A question (for instance, on the semantics of a program) with Boolean
answer is
• Decidable if and only if there exists an algorithm that takes the program as input and effectively computes the answer to the question
in finite time;
• Semidecidable if and only if there exists an algorithm that takes the
program as input and effectively computes the answer to the question in finite time when the answer is true and may be not terminating when it is false;
• Undecidable if and only if there exists no algorithm that takes the program as input and effectively computes the answer to the question
in finite time (any algorithm providing correct answers will therefore answer true, false, I don’t know, or will not terminate).
Turing’s theorem 9.1 states that the halting/termination problem is algorithmically undecidable. Rice’s theorem 9.12 states that the problem of
whether a program has a given nontrivial semantic property is algorithmically undecidable. Our proofs are informal sketches in the style of Neil
Jones [537] and Bernhard Reus [825]; see [841, 902] for rigorous proofs.

114

9.2

Turing Completeness

A programming language is Turing complete if and only if it is possible
to write an interpreter for this language in this language. For example,
a language without iteration or recursion is not Turing complete since it
cannot read arbitrarily long programs.
A programming language is deterministic if any input (i.e., given initial
values of variables) has a unique outcome (including the possibility of
nontermination). The language of chapters 4 and 7 is deterministic.
The language of chapters 4 and 7 is Turing complete (because the initial
values of variables are not sequences of characters but integers, an interpreter written in this language would have to encode programs as naturals, for example, the natural obtained by concatenating the fixed-size
character codes of the sequence of characters constituting the program).

9.3

Undecidability of the Termination Problem

The halting/termination problem is to write a program termination that
takes as input an arbitrary program P (represented as a string or file or an
integer encoding) and its input data D (also represented as a string or file
or an integer encoding) such that termination(P,D) always terminates
for all programs P and input data D and returns tt if the execution of the
program P on the data D does terminate and ff if the execution of the
program P on the data D does not terminate.
The halting/termination problem is undecidable because no such algorithm does exist. The proof of the halting/termination problem undecidability is credited to Alan Turing [931, 932]. Similar arguments had been
used to prove undecidability of other problems (e.g.„ in number theory
by Alonzo Church [184] or the incompleteness theorems in logic by Kurt
Gödel [420]), but the originality of Turing is that his theorem explicitly
refers to the halting problem of a (Turing) machine modeling computers.
Theorem 9.1 (Turing’s theorem) The halting/termination problem is
undecidable for a deterministic Turing complete language.
Proof Sketch The proof that such a program termination cannot exist
is by reductio ad absurdum. Let interpret be an interpreter for the language such that interpret(P,D) is the result of running the program P
on the input data D.
Assume termination does exist. Define the deterministic program
contradiction
function P = if (termination(P,P)) { while (tt); }

and run the program contradiction on its own text, that is,
115

contradiction(contradiction).

More precisely, that is computed by running the interpreter
interpret(contradiction,contradiction).

Then termination(contradiction, contradiction) is computed by
running the interpreter
interpret(termination, (contradiction,contradiction))

and always terminates.
• If contradiction(contradiction) does terminate then
termination(contradiction, contradiction)

terminates and returns true, which is a contradiction because the iteration while (tt); does not terminate or
• contradiction(contradiction) does not terminate and then
termination(contradiction, contradiction)

terminates and returns false, which is a contradiction because the iteration while (tt); is not entered and the program terminates.
A more rigorous proof must precisely define what is a program and what
is the execution of this program, for which Alonzo Church introduced the
lambda calculus and Alan Turing introduced the notion of Turing machine. Equivalently, we can formally define the semantics of programs,
which is the objective of chapter 7, “Maximal Trace Semantics.”

9.4 Examples of Algorithmically Undecidable Problems
Other decision problems for programs can be proved undecidable by reduction to the halting/termination problem.
Example 9.2 (constancy) Constancy analysis (see exercise 3.45) is the
problem of deciding whether a program P assigns a value different from
the initial value 0 to a variable x. It is undecidable because otherwise,
given a program P, consider a fresh variable x not in P and the witness
program P′ = P; x = 1 ;. P′ assigns a value different from the initial value 0 to
the variable x if and only if P terminates. Hence if the constancy problem
were decidable, termination would also be decidable, in contradiction to
Turing’s theorem 9.1.
Exercise 9.3 (absence of runtime error) Prove that the problem of
proving the absence of runtime error in an execution of a program P is
undecidable.
116

Exercise 9.4 (sign) Prove that the problem of deciding whether a numerical variable has a given sign is undecidable.
Exercise 9.5 (type) Prove that the problem of deciding whether a variable has a given type is undecidable (it follows that the more difficult typing problem of inferring the type of a variable is also undecidable).
Corollary 9.6 (failures of algorithms “solving” undecidable problems) Let A(P, d) be an algorithm to solve an undecidable problem
on program P for input data d. Assume that the algorithm is sound (otherwise, giving wrong answers is easy). Soundness means that A(P,d) correctly answers true, false, or fails, that is, answers I don’t know or does not
terminate.
Then A(P,d) must fail on infinitely many input data d.
Proof By reductio ad absurdum, assume that A(P,d) fails on finitely
many input data di , i Δ only. Then ask mathematicians to solve these
finitely many problems and provide an Answer(P,di ) {true,false}. Formally check the correctness of their answers for each of di , i Δ, with a
proof assistant or theorem prover.

Semidecidability

A problem with Boolean answer is semidecidable if and only if there exists
an algorithm that terminate with true when the answer is true and might
not terminate when the answer is false.
Example 9.7 (termination) The termination problem is semidecidable. Simply run the program and answer true upon termination. If the
program does not terminate then there is no answer that is allowed by
semidecidability.

9.6

Rice’s Theorem

As shown by example 9.2 and exercises 9.3, 9.4, and 9.5 the proof that a
specific program semantic property is undecidable is always by the same
reduction to the nontermination problem that was proved to be undecidable in section 9.3. Rice’s theorem [830] is a generalization from these particular semantics properties to all nontrivial semantic properties: Rice’s
theorem states that all nontrivial semantic properties of programs are undecidable.

The following exercise shows, using Rice’s theorem, that precise static
analysis is infeasible.
Exercise 9.13 Prove that there is no algorithm for examining a program

defined for n).
Rice’s theorem 9.12 remains valid when restricting the considered programs (e.g.„ programs of a given complexity class [55]).

9.7

Conclusion

By Rice’s theorem 9.12, checking that a program semantics has any nontrivial semantic property is undecidable. This means that when a sound
algorithm automatically checks for a program’s properties, the algorithm
may not terminate; or if it always terminates, then either there are restrictions on the considered programs (such as finite states only, e.g.„ model
checking), a human interaction is necessary (e.g.„ theorem proving), or
the result may be true, false, or undetermined, that is, I don’t know. This
is an indication that the verification and static program analysis problems
are very difficult, even with approximate solutions [613], but not impossible, although without limit on the perfection of verification and static
program analysis.
Rice’s theorem 9.12 was extended to program verification and analysis by [277] to show that, from a computability perspective, and for
infinite abstract properties, static program analysis is harder than checking/verification. Another extension in [74] is to abstract semantics more
general than the extensional/functional semantics property of Rice’s
theorem 9.12.

also be decidable, which is a contradiction.

Posets, Lattices, and Complete Lattices
Partial order theory emerged from the work of George Boole, Ernst
Schröder, Charles Peirce, and it was mainly developed by Garrett
Birkhoff [120]. Partial order theory is an abstraction of set theory in
which
is expressed in terms of
and
(e.g., property implication)
is abstracted as a partial order
(e.g., abstract property implication).
The abstract partial order
retains the essential properties of inclusion (reflexive, antisymmetric, and transitive). Many theorems of set
theory remain valid, but not all, and this widely broadens the scope of
applicability of order theory (see introductions in [121, 295, 445]). The
poset representation ℙ,
of program properties ℙ with an abstract
implication provides a unified theory of program properties and their
abstraction while giving us much more freedom and diversity in the
choice of the possible encodings of abstract properties.

Duality Principle

The order dual of an order-theoretic definition or statement is obtained
by replacing by its inverse , upper by lower, least by greatest, by ,
by , join by meet, meet by join, maximum by minimum, and so forth.
The duality principle states that if a definition or statement is valid for all
partially ordered sets then the dual definition or dual statement is also
valid for all partially ordered sets [121].

be increasing that is, x, y A

10.10

Conclusion

Abstract program properties can be represented by posets. Finite Boolean
lattices appeared in dataflow analysis [27, 29]. Gary Kildall [572] (and independently, Ben Wegbreit [967]) introduced the use of non-Boolean fi128

nite lattices in dataflow analysis. Gary Kildall [572] required the lattice to
be distributive, which is not true of his main example: constant propagation. In many examples of dataflow analysis, lattices are used dually, the
infimum is tt(true) and the supremum is ff( ) [472]. Hassan Aït-Kaci et
al. [15] provides an example of efficient implementation of finite lattices.
The use of complete lattices not satisfying the increasing chain condition
(every strictly increasing chain is finite) in program static analysis was
introduced in [234, 235].

Galois Connections and Abstraction
Galois connections (or Galois adjunctions) formalize the correspondence
between concrete properties (e.g., sets of traces) and abstract properties
(e.g., sets of reachable states) in case there is always a most precise abstract property overapproximating any concrete property.

Galois Correspondences

A Galois correspondence is a Galois connection
,
,
, that
is, the adjoint functions are decreasing with 1
α ˚ γ and 1
γ ˚ α. So
a Galois correspondence is the semidual of a Galois connection. Their
composition is not a Galois correspondence but is a Galois connection. It
is the original notion inherited from Evarist Galois’ work.
We prefer Galois connections because they compose.
Galois correspondences are sometimes called decreasing Galois connections. Many other alternative names can be found in the literature, for
example, residuated mappings for Galois connections [128, section 1.3]
and Galois connections for Galois correspondences [128, section 1.6].

Moore Families

By theorem 11.88, the image of a complete lattice by a closure operator
is closed by arbitrary meets. A subset ℳ ℘( ) of a poset
,
that is
closed by arbitrary meets (i.e., S ℳ. S exists in

and S ℳ
) is called a Moore family (after [713]). So, by the dual of exercise 10.7, a
Moore family ℳ,
is a complete lattice (which includes the supremum
=
of the poset ,
for the meet of the empty set).
Reciprocally, a Moore family of a complete lattice uniquely defines a closure operator (exercise 11.89), that is to say, an abstraction. Hence an abstraction can be uniquely defined by choosing an arbitrary subset of the
concrete properties and then completing it to a Moore family by adding
missing meets (including the supremum).

11.17

Conclusion

We can represent abstract program properties by posets and, in case of
existence of a best abstraction, establish the correspondence with the concrete properties using a Galois connection. The concrete order structure
is preserved in the abstract and inversely. Otherwise stated, concrete and
abstract implications coincide up to the Galois connection. Hence proofs
in the abstract domain
,
using the abstract implication/order are
valid in the concrete ,
for , up to this Galois connection.
The original definition of Galois correspondences originating from the
work of Evarist Galois [388] were between powersets and decreasing
℘(C),
℘(A),
so they do not compose as their semidual
Galois connections. The order-theoretical Galois connection is credited
to Oystein Ore [762] (spelled connexion). Galois connections have numerous applications in mathematics [309], including number theory [609],
modal logic [344], fuzzy logic [159, 949], fuzzy sets [993], μ-calculus [132],
topology [19], metric spaces [154], formal concept analysis [394, 600],
computability [146], constraint satisfaction problems [382, 383], entropy
in thermodynamics [607], and others. Galois connections [492, 554] and
closure operators [167] have been generalized in category theory. One
can also study pairs of functions α, γ with α increasing/decreasing, γ
increasing/decreasing, γ ˚ α which is extensive/reductive, and α ˚ γ which
is reductive/extensive; Galois connections being for the first choice [106,
281, 341, 364, 680].
The results on Galois connections apply to preorders (reflexive and transitive) when partially ordered up to the equivalence x
y (x y y
x), in which case equalities must be replaced by the equivalence
.
Abstract interpretation with best abstraction has many equivalent formalizations equivalent to Galois connections [241]. For example, Moore families (exercise 11.89), closure operators (exercise 11.61), covers (exercise
11.10), logical relations [828], and soundness relations [738]. The advantage of Galois connections is that the abstraction α is explicit (and useful in
discussing completeness) and abstract properties may be different from
the concrete properties.
Logical relations are mathematically equivalent to Galois connections
(section 11.14) and so can be used to establish the soundness of verification methods, static analyses, and types [738, 828].
Completeness involves considering the best abstraction given in section
11.12. By (11.84), this best abstraction involves considering all possible
overapproximations specified by the logical relation, which is impractical
(a point made in [249] and misinterpreted in [60], in which completeness
is not considered). This is also the problem with completeness whenever
155

considering only a concretization function, using lemma 11.42 to determine the best abstraction (e.g., [546] provides no completeness proof of
Hoare logic). This situation is further studied in [245].
The combinations of Galois connections in section 11.13 can be extended
to a Galois connection calculus [264] to build complex Galois connections
out of basic ones. As shown in the following chapters, a proof method or
a static analysis is uniquely defined by a program semantics and a Galois
connection.

Relational and Transformer Semantics
We abstract the finite and infinite trace semantics into relational semantics and then into transformer semantics, generalizing the weakest predicate transformers. This is an illustration of Galois connections.

By property of variables x, one understands a property of their values ρ(x)
as given by an environment ρ. Therefore, a set P ℘( ) of environments
defines a property of variables that is a relation between their possible
values, stating that the values ρ(x) of variables x should be such that ρ
P.

+ 1}. This makes explicit that in a program, a variable x denotes in fact
its value ρ(x) given by the state ρ of the computer memory. Such properties are called relational because they can express relations between the
values of variables.

Weakest Preconditions

The weakest preconditions introduced by Edger W. Dijkstra [321, 327] use
logical predicates and so cannot refer to nontermination directly. It is
however possible to handle non/termination indirectly by postulating the
existence of a weakest precondition (wp[S]Q excluding the possibility of
nontermination) and weakest liberal precondition (wlp[S]Q including the
possibility of nontermination) for a statement to satisfy a postproperty Q
{ } and Q
upon termination. They can be defined as follows (Q
).
For brevity, we write post[S] for post R S , etc. We also write gwp S Q
(respectively wp S Q, wlp S ) for gwp R S (respectively wp R S ,
wlp R S ).

By definition wlp S tt = tt (truth tt is ) and wlp S ff wp S tt = ff

= wlp S Q wp S tt.
Edger W. Dijkstra observed [322] that a deterministic statement either (a)
terminates with a final environment satisfying a given postproperty Q, or
(b) terminates with a final environment not satisfying the given postproperty Q, or (c) does not terminate. For a nondeterministic system, Edger W.
Dijkstra [321] characterizes the possible behaviors as the following:
(a) Execution of S will terminate in a final environment satisfying Q
(gwp[S]Q).

Figure 206:
(b) Execution of S will terminate in a final environment satisfying ¬Q (i.e.,
Q, gwp[S]¬Q).

Figure 207:
(c) Execution of S will fail to terminate properly (gwp[R]{ }).
(ab) Execution of S will terminate properly but the initial environment
does not determine whether the final environment will satisfy Q or not
(gwp[S]tt).
(ac) Execution of S may terminate, in which case the final environment
will satisfy Q but the initial environment does not determine whether S
will terminate or not (gwp[S](Q { })).
(bc) Execution of S may terminate, in which case the final environment
will not satisfy Q but the initial environment does not determine whether
S will terminate or not (gwp[S](¬Q { })).
(abc) The initial environment does not determine whether S will terminate or not and upon termination, if ever, whether the final environment
will satisfy Q or not (gwp[S](tt { }).

12.6

Conclusion

The relational semantics R+ is an abstraction of the trace semantics + .
The abstract semantics R abstracts away termination (and could be
called the natural semantics after [551]). The trace semantics + itself
is essentially a relation between an initialization trace and a finite or
infinite continuation semantics in the spirit of [686].
Predicate transformers where introduced in mathematics by Jacques
Riguet [831, p. 118]. See [918] for a generalization.
They were rediscovered in computer science. The weakest/backward/abductive
preconditions are from [321], and the strongest/forward/deductice postconditions are found in [235, 241, 328]. Their definition as abstractions
are from [222, 502] and [227] in which it is suggested to add nontermination to predicates for better expressivity. The special case of total and
deterministic relations (exercise 12.17) is considered in [222].
Abstract interpretation was originally introduced [235, 241] using predicate transformers (called deductive semantics in [235]). The advantage
is that the formulation is language independent. For example, it directly
applies to Prolog [205]. The disadvantage is that it is sometimes too abstract (see, for example, chapter 44, “Software Model Checking”) and the
instantiation of the concepts for a specific language may not look simple.
It remains to provide a structural definition of these semantics. This is
carried out in chapter 25, “Abstract Reachability / Invariance / Safety Ver-

Figure 213:
173

Figure 214:
ification Semantics,” and chapter 26, “Hoare Logic,” for partial correctness, namely case (ac) of section 12.4. Structural backward transformers
are considered in chapter 50, “Backward Accessibility Semantics.”

13
Topology
A topology can be thought of as abstracting away all properties irrelevant
to the notion of limit (of functions, sequences, etc.). Topology is related to
program trace semantics because infinite traces have been defined as the
limit of prefix closed semantics (7.2). This limit could have been defined
in topological terms (see example 13.11). We will use topology in chapter
14 to discuss program properties that do (liveness) or do not (safety) depend on this passage to the limit in the trace semantics. This chapter is a
very lightweight introduction to topology; [53, 137, 890] are much more
detailed introductions to topology.

safety and liveness trace properties.

14
Safety and Liveness Trace Properties
Safety properties are trace properties that can be checked at runtime. Examples are absence of runtime error or that the successive values taken
by a variable are increasing. Liveness properties are trace properties
that cannot be checked at runtime. Examples are termination or guarantee that the value of an integer variable eventually reach 0. Any trace
property is the intersection of a safety and a liveness property [32]. Some
program properties (like dependency studied in chapter 47) are not trace
properties so are neither a safety nor a liveness nor the intersection of a
safety and liveness property.

Intuition for Safety

Safety properties S of programs are trace properties so that S ℘( + × + )
(and, by section 8.6, are the abstraction α (8.8) of semantic properties in

The characteristics of a safety property S is that any program execution

Example 14.1 The property “the program never divides by zero” is a
safety property because the violation “the program eventually divides by
zero” can be proved at runtime by testing for a division by zero and waiting long enough. How long is unknown, but definitely finite in case of
violation.
The program property “all executions do terminate” (that is, + P
( + × + )) is not a safety property because if the program has not yet terminated in a prefix computation, it does not mean that it will terminate
later or will never terminate. The violation of the termination property
is “some execution never terminates,” which is not observable in finite
time, so this is not a safety property.
The violation of a safety property by a given trace is checkable at runtime,
but its verification is another story. There might be infinitely many different finite traces and infinite ones, so an exhaustive search of possible
violations is hopeless, as shown by Rice’s theorem 9.12.

14.2

is, an eventuality/guarantee property. We show that this reduction of liveness to guarantee is improper.

14.5

Conclusion

This book concentrates on the verification and static analysis of safety
properties of programs.
194

The safety/liveness classification of trace properties is credited to [32, 33]
(see also [1, 611, 863]) with a topological presentation in [133, 654, 960].
The guarantee properties are part of Zohar Manna and Amir Pnueli’s [170,
650, 651] hierarchy of weak liveness/progress properties. Reduction of
some liveness properties to safety (exercise 14.43) has been studied, for
example, by [118, 772, 867]. Topological presentations of abstract interpretation can be found in [238, 858, 859].

Solution to exercise 14.24 The infinite union of safety properties is not
a safety property. For example, terminating in exactly n steps is a safety
property. To check it at runtime, simply count the number of steps and
produce an alarm after n steps. Their infinite union is termination, which
is not a safety property. By theorem 14.15, the safety properties form a
complete lattice αsafety (℘( + × + )), , , + × + , S αlimit (S),
(because
the join of prefix closed traces is prefix closed). Therefore the intersection
of safety properties is a safety property and the limit of their unions, not
their union, is the lub. In the example, the union is termination but the
limit of termination introduces the possibility of nontermination.

FIXPOINTS AND THEIR ABSTRACTIONS
Fixpoints are the mathematical formalization of iteration and recursion
(chapter 15).
They provide the rigorous foundations of the deductive systems used to
describe semantics (chapter 16) and can replace them in the descriptions
of semantics (chapter 17).
The abstraction of fixpoints (chapter 18) is the basis for the design of more
abstract semantics and static analyzers.

S

• 1. reach a fixpoint f p = f (f p );
• 2. or reach a cycle and iterate forever along that cycle f p+ℓ = f p , ℓ >
0;
• 3. or iterate forever along infinitely many different elements p ≠ q .
f p ≠ f q . This is impossible if the set S is finite.
We study sufficient conditions on S, f, and a, ensuring that the iteration
reaches a fixpoint.

15.4

Conclusion

The idea of solving equations iteratively dates back to the Isaac Newton –
Joseph Raphson method [751, 820]. The study of fixpoints originates from
the principle of mathematical induction for chains by Richard Dedekind
[302], Ernst Zermelo set theory [1001], and Gerhard Hessenberg [494]
study for reductive or, equivalently, extensive functions x L.x f (x).1
This idea of iteration has produced numerous fixpoint theorems such
as that of Casimir Kuratowski [603, Théorème II], Stefan Banach [83,
Théorème 6], and Leonid Kantorovitch [555, theorem I] for increasing
functions on bounded posets, and others.
Tarski’s theorem is often called Knaster-Tarski’s theorem because Bronisław Knaster (mentioning that the results were obtained in common
with Tarski) previously proved a weaker version for powersets of a set
[584]; see exercise 15.17. The iterative version of theorem 15.26 is in [925,
p. 305] for complete join morphisms (i.e., f ( i Δ xi ) = i Δ f (xi )), indeed
countable ones. It was extended by Dana Scott to upper continuity [870]
and to increasing functions using transfinite iterations, [136, ch. III,
example 6b, p. 48] and [5, 240, 656]. This result is often attributed to
Stephen Cole Kleene, after its first recursion theorem [582, p. 348].2

16.4

Inductive Definitions

Inductive definitions are mathematical generalizations of recursive programs such as the factorial f(0) = 1 and f(n) = n *f(n − 1) for n ℤ.

Figure 255:
The difference is that at each recursive call a different function is called
which parameters are all previously computed values.
Of course programmers would implement F n ( D(i), i [0,n − 1] ) by a
function F taking n as a parameter of F and D(i), i [0,n − 1] represented,
for example, as a linear list of n elements.
The program might not terminate for negative values of the parameter, in
which case the corresponding mathematical definition is not well defined.
Termination can be proved by recurrence. For n = 0, the function f returns the evaluation of expression 1, which terminates. Assume, by re213

Figure 256:

Figure 257:
currence hypothesis that f(n) terminates. For the parameter n + 1, the
function call returns the evaluation of (n + 1) ×f((n + 1) − 1). Because f(n)
terminates by induction hypothesis, the evaluation of the expression terminates. By recurrence, all calls f(n), n ℕ do terminate. The corresponding reasoning on the mathematical inductive definition is by induction on
a given well founded relation ( is on ℕ for the factorial example).
Of course, computer integers are limited in size which leads to errors.

Figure 258:
The corresponding mathematical reasoning must consider the universe
𝕌 = [INT_MIN, INT_MAX] from C directive #include <limits.h>, not
= ℤ.

Coinductive Definitions

definitions by theorems 16.12 and 16.16 in section 16.3, coinductive definitions are equivalent to greatest fixpoint definitions.

Bi-inductive Definitions

Although finite and infinite traces of program semantics can be defined
as coinductive definition/greatest fixpoints (see exercise 16.36), it is often
more practical (in particular for fixpoint abstraction in chapter 18, “Fixpoint Abstraction”) to define finite traces as least fixpoint (thus constructing longer and longer ones) and infinite traces as greatest fixpoint (thus
eliminating the ones with longer and longer unfitting prefixes instead of
passing to the limit as in chapter 7, “Maximal Trace Semantics”). This can
be done with bi-inductive definitions thus avoiding having to consider
finite and infinite traces separately.

16.8

Conclusion

Fixpoint, deductive, and inductive definitions are used to provide well
defined specifications of the structural semantics of programs and their
abstractions. Context-free grammars are a particular case (see exercise
16.15 and [181, 419, 868]). An overview of set-theoretic formal definitions
is given in [6]. A generalization from ℘( ) to complete partial orders is
considered in [250].
Coinduction originates from [7], [686], and category theory [8]. Biinductive definitions are from [247, 260].
Another interpretation
219

between induction and coinduction considers infinite proof trees [285]
that are regular [219], that is, containing only finitely many different
subtrees.

Structural Fixpoint Prefix and Maximal Trace

equivalent fixpoint form. It follows that structural inductive semantics
such as the prefix trace semantics of section 6.3 and the maximal trace
semantics of section 7.3 have equivalent structural fixpoint presentations
that we study in this chapter 17.

17.3

Conclusion

The first semantics using fixpoint definitions were the denotational semantics of Dana Scott and Christopher Strachey [871, 872]. In fact, all
program semantics can be given fixpoint definitions (by abstract interpretations of fixpoint trace semantics [227]).
The correctness/soundness proof of any static analysis must relate the results of the analysis to a formal definition of the executions of any program of a given programming language. Maximal traces are a rather pre-

229

cise descriptions of these executions (although e.g., they abstract away
execution times) so are a good basis for abstracting into less precise descriptions of program executions (like the reachability semantics of chapter 19) with respect to which static analyses can be proved sound (and so,
by composition, are also sound with respect to traces). But some static
analyses such at [200, 263, 804, 906] can be proved only with respect to
traces (because any abstractions of traces (e.g.„ as a reachability semantics of chapter 19) would not be precise enough).
1. 1 The definiendum (plural definienda) is the subject of a definition,
what is being defined.
2. 2 The definiens (plural definientia) is the term/symbolic expression
that defines the definiendum.

Exact and Approximate Greatest Fixpoint Abstraction
By duality, including for Galois connections in n lemma 11.25, the exact
and approximate least fixpoint abstract theorems of sections 18.2, 18.3,
and 18.4 apply dually to greatest fixpoint underapproximation for the concretization γ. However, as shown in chapter 50, it is sometimes necessary
to overapproximate greatest fixpoints for the abstraction α. In that case,
the commutation condition of corollary 18.35 is sufficient to ensure an
exact/complete least fixpoint abstraction, but not for the greatest fixpoint,
as shown by the following counterexample.
Nevertheless, the following results can be applied.

VI
REACHABILITY SEMANTICS
The forward/deductive reachability semantics of a syntactically correct
program is an abstraction of its trace semantics specifying the set of states
reachable at any program point for all executions of the program (chapter
19). It is an invariant property of the program executions.
Because it is an abstraction of the trace semantics, it can be formally derived from this semantics by calculational design (chapter 20).

19
Structural Forward Reachability Semantics
The (forward/deductive) reachability semantics of a program is an abstraction of the prefix trace semantics. The assertional reachability semantics
S attaches to each program point ℓ labs S of a statement
S a set
S ℓ of environments that may be encountered during any execution of the statement S reaching that program point. The environments
record the values of the program variables whenever reaching that point.
The relational reachability semantics
S is a variant where the values of variables at a program point are related to the initial values of variables.

Structural Forward Reachability Semantics

We define the forward reachability semantics of a program P by structural induction on the syntax of program P. The definition is postulated,
that is, claimed to be true without justification. This justification will be
presented in chapter 20, “Calculational Design of the Forward Reachability Semantics.”
The forward reachability semantics of assignment has already been postulated at (19.12) and that of iteration at (19.16).
The forward reachability semantics of a program P ::= S l ℓ′ is that of its
statement list S l.

that the reachable environments are the initial environments.

environments to themselves because they are not modified.

Figure 329:
The forward reachability semantics of a conditional statement S ::= if (B)
St is the set of reachable environments in St under the hypothesis that
the test B is true and, after the conditional statement, the union of the
environments reaching the end of the true alternative St and those for
which the conditional statement is skipped when the test B is false.
Reachability of a conditional statement S ::= if (B) St

The forward reachability semantics of a conditional statement S ::= if (B)
St else Sf is the set of reachable environments in St under the hypothesis
that the test B is true, the set of reachable environments in Sf under the
hypothesis that the test B is false, and, after the conditional statement, the
union of the environments reaching the end of the true alternative St or
that of the false alternative Sf .

19.5

Uncomputability of the Reachability Semantics

It is possible, but in practice difficult, to calculate the reachable environments by hand for iteration. This computation would be better fully automated. By Rice’s theorem 9.12, this is impossible. The following lesser-evil
solutions have been considered:
• The set
is assumed to be finite (e.g.„ all variables are Boolean or
is finite). So elements of ℘( ϱ ) have finite computer representations. The reachability semantics
while ℓ (B) Sb can be encoded
and computed with finite time and memory resources. This is, depending on the way elements of ℘( ϱ ) are represented, enumerative or symbolic model checking [193]. The finiteness hypothesis is
restrictive and the unsolved problem is state explosion as shown by
examples as trivial as exercise 3.48.
• Ask the programmer to provide the semantics
while ℓ (B) Sb
0
or an inductive approximation of this semantics and check that it is
correct by applying a proof method of chapter 25 using a theorem
prover, for example, [562] or a proof assistant, for example, [210,
754]).
• Use an abstract interpretation to simplify the semantics
while
ℓ (B) Sb
and
then
use
one
of
the
previous
techniques
(e.g.„
ab0
stract model checking) or effectively compute the simplified semantics (e.g.„ static analysis).
By corollary 9.6, all these methods will fail on infinitely many programs.
Their practical effectiveness measured as scalability and precision can
only, up to now, be determined experimentally. [] is a first formal attempt
