19.7

Conclusion

The forward reachability semantics ignores all aspects of trace properties irrelevant to reachability. It is therefore a collecting semantics for
reachability/invariance properties. This means that it is the most abstract
of the abstract semantics that are precise enough to express reachability/invariance properties. Therefore it is the basis for designing invariance proof methods and can be further abstracted to get automatic static
reachability program analysis methods.
The forward reachability semantics has been postulated in this chapter
19. It will be proved correct by calculational design in the following chapter 20. It can also be specified as a solution to a system of equations or
constraints, as shown in chapter 23.

20.5

Conclusion

Abstract interpretation can be used to relate semantics at various levels
of abstraction describing executions with more or fewer details [227]. As
illustrated by this chapter 20, the formal definition of the concrete semantics and the abstraction can be used to design the abstract semantics by
calculus, using fixpoint abstraction given in chapter 18.
The forward reachability semantics is the basis for invariance proof methods and can be further abstracted to get automatic static reachability program analysis methods.

VII
ABSTRACT DOMAIN AND ABSTRACT INTERPRETER
The program semantics can be abstracted away in a mathematical structure given by an abstract domain (formalizing the program properties
defined by the semantics) and an abstract interpreter (formalizing how
the semantics can be calculated), chapter 21.
This abstract interpreter is a formal specification of a generic static analyzer parameterized by an abstract domain.
This abstract interpreter can be understood as providing the solutions to
equations (chapter 23) computed by iteration and by passing to the limit
(chapter 22).

of chapter 19 all have the same structure. They are instances

interpreter parameterized by an abstract domain representing the information collected about program executions and the basic operations involved in this collection.

21.3

Finitary Abstract Domains

An abstract domain ℙ¤ is finitary when it satisfies the increasing chain condition, that is, any strictly ¤ -increasing chain is finite. A finite abstract
domain is finitary.
Theorem 21.24

The abstract interpreter (i.e., a program implementing

the specification ¤ ) is computationally well defined (i.e., terminating) for
finitary abstract domains.
Proof By theorem 21.16, ¤ is mathematically well defined. By hypothesis the elements of ℙ¤ are computer representable. But fixpoint iterations
might be infinite (e.g., for the reachability semantics of a nonterminating
program). However, the abstract domain being finitary the least fixpoint
can be computed by iteration from the infimum.
Note that only the fixpoint iteration strictly increasing chains need to be
finite (so the definition of finitary can be weakened to the iterates of fixpoints).

Conclusion

The idea of an abstract interpreter is from [572, 741, 899, 967] and [234].
Infinitary abstract domains and the notion of soundness with respect to
an operational semantics were first introduced in [234]. Abstract domains
302

and abstract interpreter are available online such as APRON/Interproc
[897] (see section 53.2.8). Abstract domain
[528, 529], PPL [69] and
can be integrated in constraint solvers [791, 921]. [972] shows how to
transform an abstract interpreter into an abstract compiler [134] by partial evaluation [538], [257, sect. 7] using the first Futamura projection
[384].

22
Chaotic Iterations
An alternative to structural definitions of semantics is to use solutions to
systems of equations. Chaotic iterations for solving systems of equations
allow to choose at each iteration which components evolve while the others are unchanged (but none can be forgotten forever). In full generality,
different iteration strategies lead to different results. On the contrary, for
continuous equations on complete partial orders, the limit of the iterates
is always the least fixpoint.

22.3

Chaotic Iterations

For solving systems of linear equations, Daniel Chazan and Willard Miranker proposed a generalization to chaotic relaxation. A simple instance
for general systems of equations is chaotic iterations. At each step, one
can arbitrarily choose which components do evolve with the fairness condition that no component is omitted forever. If all components evolve at
each iteration, that is Jacobi iterations. If the components evolve one after
another, that is Gauss-Seidel.

307

Figure 421:
A chaotic iteration is defined by an infinite sequence ℑ of subsets of {1, …,
n} specifying that all components in ℑ(k) should evolved at iterate k (while
those in {1, …, n} ℑ(k) remain unchanged). This choice must be fair (i.e.,
no component is forgotten forever).

Conclusion

Chaotic iterations cover all iteration algorithms used to solve systems
of equations in static analysis, such as the work list [572]. An efficient
chaotic iterations strategy was proposed by François Bourdoncle for
static analysis [138] (the iteration strategy is also explained in [574]; see
[574, 575] for memory allocation). Static analysis by constraint resolution
amounts to a fixpoint computation by chaotic iteration [47, 251].
The chaotic iterations generalize from continuous to increasing operators
on CPOs using transfinite iterations and to asynchronous iterations where
the components evolve in parallel [220, 221]1 in order to minimize idle
times on parallel or distributed computers. In this last case the iterates
may not be increasing so without a limit in a CPO but this limit exists and is
the least fixpoint in complete lattices. Dijkstra-Scholten’s algorithm can be
used to detect convergence of asynchronous iterations [325, 326]. Parallel fixpoint computations have been experimented successfully in Astrée
[708] and Pikos [574], in both cases with good performance with four parallel threads and possibly degraded performance beyond that [447, 574].

Abstract Equational Semantics
Traditional data flow analyses are expressed as solutions to systems of
Boolean equations attached to program graphs [195, pp. 429–461], not as
an abstract structural semantics [472]. These equations are abstractions
of the structural semantics essentially losing the structural information
on programs. For example, circular dependencies appearing in equations
because of iterations must be rebuilt [195, pp. 435–437] (nowadays using
Tarjan’s strongly connected components algorithm [923]), whereas, knowing the program syntax, iterations are straightforward to locate.
A variable

ℓ is attached to each label ℓ of the program P. The equations
must be designed so that their solutions satisfy ℓ = ¤ P 0 ℓ for all pro-

Many static program analysis methods solve inequations instead of equations (e.g., [475] and the related [251], or chapter 46, among many others).
This follows from the fact that the least solution
equations

327

Z, X Y as x X.x Y, and so on, which may give the false impression
that solving such inequations is a problem quite different from solving
equations iteratively. Krzysztof Apt [47] proves the contrary. Therefore,
static analysis by constraint resolution fits perfectly in the abstract interpretation framework; see chapter 25, “Abstract Reachability / Invariance
/ Safety Verification Semantics” for an example of constraint generation.

23.4

Conclusion

The understanding of static program analysis as solving fixpoint equations associated to the program (graph) dates back from the origin of
dataflow analysis [27, 195]. This point of view is much broader and
applies equally well to semantics in part III, verification in part VIII, and
static analysis in parts IX and XI. We give more importance to the functional semantics

over the equational semantics

we prefer to reason on the solution

be reasoned upon by structural induction, and does not introduce an
intermediate step of building equations before solving them. However,

are perfectly interchangeable because they depend solely on the choice of the abstract domain of
definition 21.1 and its soundness (and completeness) of definition 27.1.

VIII
SPECIFICATION AND VERIFICATION
Program verification consists in proving that the semantics of a program
¤
P ℙ in an abstract domain ¤ satisfies a given specification ¤ P
.
¤
A verifier needs a stronger inductive invariant ℐ
satisfying verification conditions (given in chapter 25) and implying the specification ¤ P .

These verification conditions for the invariant ℐ to be true rely on fixpoint
induction (chapter 24) and are therefore sound (i.e. what is proved is true)
and complete (i.e. what is true can be proved).
Specification and verification can be presented equivalently as a program
logic (chapter 26).

331

24
Fixpoint Induction
Tarski’s fixpoint theorems provide a method for proving properties of fixpoints called fixpoint induction. Alternatively, iteration induction is a fixpoint proof method based on fixpoint iteration. Both proof methods are
sound and complete. They provide the underlying principles of formal
methods for proving program correctness.

24.3

Conclusion

Fixpoint induction in theorem 24.1 directly follows from Tarski’s fixpoint
theorem 15.6, as observed by [777, (2.0.2)], [778, (2.3)], and [221, p. 3.4.1].
It relies on properties of f above its least fixpoint. In contrast, iteration
induction directly follows from Scott–Kleene’s fixpoint theorem 15.26, as
observed by [648, 652, 869]. It relies on properties of f below its least fixpoint. Iteration induction generalizes to transfinite iterations [240]. Dual
coinduction theorems can be easily stated (see section 10.4). As a direct
application, proof methods for verifying semantic properties of programs
are by induction on the fixpoint definition of these semantics [232, 243].

Abstract Reachability / Invariance / Safety Verification Semantics
The invariance proof method of Alan Turing [933], Peter Naur [742] and
Bob Floyd [376] essentially consist in asking the programmer to provide
an assertional invariant (or relational, for Zohar Manna [647]) and checking verification conditions that ensure that this invariant is implied by
the assertional (or relational) reachability semantics.
This invariance proof method is an application of the fixpoint induction
theorem 24.1 to the fixpoint equations of chapter 23 for the forward
reachability semantics of chapter 19. By fixpoint induction theorem
24.1, the proof method is sound (correct) and complete (always applicable) although, by Rice’s theorem 9.12, undecidable (i.e., not fully
automatizable).
We present a structural definition of the verification conditions that proceeds by induction on the program syntax in the spirit of Tony Hoare’s
logic [501] or Edger W. Dijkstra’s [321] predicate transformers. Moreover,
we do not consider the particular case of reachable states but instead consider any abstract domain for the equational semantics of chapter 23, or
equivalently the abstract semantics of chapter 21. It follows that the proof
method is sound for all possible abstractions of the abstract semantics of
chapter 21. In particular, when instantiating with the prefix trace semantics, we get a structural proof method [263, section 6] for safety specification section 14.1.

25.4

Automation of Program Verification

Automated program verification of a program component S for initial precondition 0 requires the end user to provide an inductive invariant ℐ
(at least for at S and loops because the other ones can be formally derived using the verification conditions). The abstract domain ¤ is most
often chosen to be a logic (that is a set of logical formulas closed by , ,
¤
etc.). Then the checking of the verification conditions
S
0 ℐ essentially consist in proving implications between logical formulas of ¤ , as
specified by (25.12)–(25.21). These implications are proved by a theorem
prover specialized in this logic ¤ , hopefully fully automatically. There
are several theoretical and practical difficulties.
• The theorem prover might not be able to prove valid implications.
This is why the abstract domain ¤ is often chosen to be a reduced
350

product of decidable theories (see example 36.32). By restricting expressivity, implication becomes decidable, as for satisfiability modulo theories (SMT)-solvers [91], although not necessarily in guaranteed reasonable time.
• However, the inductive invariant ℐ may not be strong enough to do
the proof.
– For decidable theories, the theorem prover/SMT-solver will provide a counterexample. This can help provide a stronger invariant.
– For undecidable theories, the theorem prover will fail to prove
the implications. The end user must understand that the inductive invariant is too weak and must provide a stronger one.
• However, the abstract domain ¤ might not be expressive enough
to express this stronger invariant. Then there is no way out, except
to use a more powerful theorem prover for a more expressive logic,
which may end up to be undecidable.
• If ¤ is very general such as a first-order logic with arithmetics used
in Isabelle genetic proof assistant, the Prototype Verification System (PVS) [771], or the Computational Logic for Applicative Common Lisp (ACL2) [561, 714], then the implication ¤ is undecidable
(by Gödel’s incompleteness theorems [420]; see theorem 9.1). Therefore the theorem prover must be helped to do the implication proofs,
a nontrivial task that often requires understanding the algorithms
used by the theorem prover and why they fail.
• An alternative consists of providing the proof by hand (or at least
the essential arguments) and have this proof automatically checked
by a proof verifier such as COQ [520].
• A final difficulty is that the inductive invariant is generally as complex as the program and the proof an order of magnitude more complex. The program, the inductive invariant, and the proof must be
maintained for modification which may be a fantastic task.
Example 25.32 (Presburger arithmetics) Presburger arithmetics is a
first-order logic with constants 0 and 1, addition +, equality =, logical operation (nand), and quantifiers and over variables. The axiomatization
(0 = x +1), x +1 = y+1 x = y, x +0 = x, and x + (y + 1) = (x + y) + 1 includes
an axiom schema providing an induction rule for proofs by recurrence
(P(0) x.(P(x) P(x+1)))
y.P(y) (where P(x) is a first-order formula in
the language of Presburger arithmetic with a free variable x (and possibly other free variables)). Presburger arithmetics is interpreted over the
naturals ℕ. Mojżesz Presburger showed that there exists an algorithm that
decides whether any given formula in the Presburger arithmetic is a theorem or is a not a theorem (and so the theory is sound [a theorem and
its negation cannot both be derived from the axioms] and complete [any
formula or its negation can be derived from the axioms]). The decision
algorithm is doubly exponential in the size n of the formula for time and
351

space [373, 760]. It is implemented in COQ [520], Z3 [299], Omega[811], and
so forth.
It is easy to write a program to compute the multiplication of two numbers
x and y (expressed as 0 + 1 + 1 + … + 1) using only Presburger arithmetics
primitives p = 0; i = 0; while (i < y) { i = i + 1; p
= p + x; }. The verification conditions of theorem 25.11 can all be
expressed in Presburger arithmetics. However Presburger arithmetics
does not contain multiplication. It is therefore impossible to prove the
correctness of this program with that abstract domain because neither the
specification (p = x × y) nor the loop invariant (p = x × i) can be expressed
in Presburger arithmetics. Of course, one can include multiplication in
the logic, but this is Peano arithmetics [787], which is undecidable [420].
Exercise 25.33 Tarski showed that the first-order theory of reals with
0, 1, +, ×, =, < is decidable (by elimination of the quantifiers and ) [927].
The decision algorithm by cylindrical algebraic decomposition [201] is implemented in Mathematica [987] and doubly exponential. Are the verification conditions for the program of example 25.32 (for integers encoded
as reals) provable in Tarski’s theory of reals?

25.5

Conclusion

We have designed by calculus the verification conditions for proving that
the reachable states imply an abstract invariance specification. This involves finding an abstract invariant and proving that is is inductive. For
reachability, this proof method is a structural version of the Alan Turing [933], Peter Naur [742], Bob Floyd [376], and Zohar Manna [647] invariance proof method. The proof method has many equivalent variants
[243] (including James Morris and Ben Wegbreit subgoal induction [323,
721] for backward reasoning).
As noticed by Bob Floyd [376], a proof method “assigns meaning to programs,” that is, define their semantics. The difference between the semantics of chapter 21, “Abstract Domain and Abstract Structural Semantics,”
chapter 23, “Abstract Equational Semantics,” and this chapter is that between increasing functions F, equations X = F(X), and inequations F(X)
X, which by Tarski fixpoint theorem 15.6 and fixpoint induction theorem 24.1 are essentially the same. Each one gives rise to a static analysis
method that looks different but is essentially equivalent, that is, computing or approximating fixpoints by iteration, solving equations, or solving
constraints [47].
One difficulty for automation is that implication is undecidable in the
proof that the inductive invariant satisfies the verification conditions.
The main difficulty however is to automatically infer an inductive invariant. Tools like Why3 [129, 371] automatically generate the verification
352

conditions, use abstract interpretation to help the user to infer part of
an inductive invariant, and resort to external provers to prove that the
user-provided inductive invariant satisfies the verification conditions.

The extended Hoare triple notation differs from the tradition [501] in that
• The T component accounts for possible break statements in the
statement S. Notice that its presence (when escape S = tt) or

– One reason for inexpressivity is the iteration. For example,
a logic with arithmetic addition operation + but missing the
multiplication × will be inexpressive, because a program can
compute a multiplication with an iteration using addition
only. Therefore × must be added to the logic for expressivity.
Then, however, exponentiation will be computable but not
expressible in the logic, etc.
– Another source of inexpressivity comes from the fact that properties of entities can be expressed in first-order logic only by
giving a name to these entities using an identifier. For example,
one can express x is odd as a first-order logic formula using 1,
+, and ×, as k . x = 2 × k + 1. However, one cannot express “to
be odd” in this logic. Some semantics can manipulate entities
that are not named by an identifier or obtained by applying selection operations from an identifier. This is the case of [539],
which directly leads to an inexpressivity result [187], which can

356

be gotten around by reasoning directly on the semantic entities
(the environment, in our case) [287, 288, 822].

26.8

Conclusion

The success of the Turing/Floyd/Naur invariance verification method of
chapter 25 is that it is the most abstract, sound, and complete invariance
proof method. Being the most abstract, it cannot be further simplified.
Being sound, it is infallible. Being complete, it is always applicable and
never fails. The success of Hoare logic is that it is a logical reformulation and, compared to previous formulations of invariance proofs, that it
works by structural induction on programs. We have used sets to encode
predicates. In practice, they are encoded using a (first-order) logic so that
the necessary inductive invariant for iteration might not be expressible
in that logic, and the logic inexpressibility is a source of incompleteness,
not Hoare logic in itself.
The original definition of Hoare logic [501] postulated rules to prove that a
Hoare triple
is valid, by structural induction on the statement
S. These rules were later proved sound and relatively complete [208, 209]
where the “relatively” means that the considered first-order logic can express the inductive invariant.
The Hoare logic that we calculated is different from the classic one [501,
503, 504] because of the break (which has led to inconsistencies [758]).
Postulating rules to derive inductive invariants [376] or valid Hoare
triples [501] is a way to “assign meaning to programs” [376], that is, to
define their semantics (called the axiomatic semantics). However, this
axiomatic semantics is too abstract for many applications such as static
analysis. For example, [46, 546] use Hoare logic as collecting semantics,
so cannot consider execution traces, and so this work cannot fully
account for the trace-based soundness of Astrée [113].
We have inferred structural Hoare logic rules defining the set ¤ S of all
valid Hoare triples for a statement S by calculational design using an abstraction αℍ

S (

¤

S ) of the structural reachability semantics

¤

S .

Although this calculational design methodology might appear superfluous for an already known logic, it is effective in designing invariance
proof methods for new languages or semantic models [24].
Program verification methods have been implemented in interactive
tools for actual programming languages. These tools often incorporate
abstract interpretation-based static analysis to help inferring inductive

369

invariants. This is the case of Frama-C for C [579] and of Key for Java [10,
chapter 6].

IX
CARTESIAN STATIC ANALYSIS
Abstractions consider program properties that are less expressive than
their semantic properties (chapter 27).
An abstraction is Cartesian when it does not relate the values of variables
(e.g., signs, parity, and constancy in chapter 3). This abstraction yields
abstract Cartesian reachability semantics, which associate with each program point a characterization of the values of the variables, but not of
their interrelationships (chapter 28). However, reduction (chapter 29)
is able to capture some of these interrelationships by iterating Cartesian
analyses.
370

As examples we provide Cartesian congruence analysis (chapter 31)
based upon elementary notions of number theory (chapter 30) and
interval/range analysis that can be performed dynamically, at runtime
(chapter 32) or statically, at compile time (chapter 33).
Because the Cartesian interval domain has infinite strictly increasing
chains, fixpoint iterations may diverge. We use interval analysis to
introduce convergence acceleration to overapproximate these fixpoints.
This study is further refined in part X.

27.1

Domain Abstraction

A concrete domain is an algebra that encodes program properties and operations on those properties. The abstraction of a concrete domain is an
abstract domain that encodes less expressive program properties and operations on these abstract properties. The relation between the concrete
and abstract domains is formalized by a concretization function and, in
the case of best abstractions, by a Galois connection. Of course, the notion of concrete and abstract domains is not absolute, but relative to the
expressiveness of one compared to the other. For example, assertional
reachability is more abstract than relational reachability, which itself is
more abstract than the maximal trace semantics.

Example: Predicate Abstraction

Predicate abstraction [437] is a simple form of abstract interpretation [80,
228]. It consists of selecting finitely many predicates {φi | i Δ} in some
logic with an associated automatic theorem prover to form the atomic
predicate of the abstract domain and closing by Boolean operations (we
choose conjunction only for this simple presentation1 ). For the sign lattice of section 3.16 that would be x 0, x ≠ 0, and x 0 for all program
variables x. All other abstract properties in the lattice are obtained by
conjunction, for example, x < 0 = x 0 x ≠ 0 and = x 0 x ≠ 0 x
0 (i.e., false in the logic). The transformers are designed by querying
an automatic theorem prover. assign¤ x, A i Θ φi , Θ Δ, is the conjunction the subset of all φj , j Δ, for which the prover can prove that
assign¤ x, A i Θ φi φj in a bounded amount of time. Otherwise the
result is
= ℤ (i.e., true in the logic). The method is similar for the
Boolean transformers test¤ B and test¤ B . Abstract properties can
be encoded as a bit vector so that the fixpoint engine of the model checker
can be reused in the abstract interpreter. Convergence of the static analysis is no problem because the lattice is finite (but can be very large). An
example is SLAM[78, 80] and its successors [683] presented as a great success but were ultimately abandoned because of the high failure rate by
timeout in an industrial environment. The whole difficulty is to select
the atomic predicates of the abstract domain. Theoretically, this amounts
to doing a proof of the program and selecting a basis for the invariants
[226]. In practice, heuristics are used; most often the basic predicates are
selected from the program text. This is very limited because interesting
invariants are not usually made explicit in the program text (as shown,
for example, by Cartesian arithmetic congruences in chapter 31 or affine
equalities in chapter 38), and many predicates extracted for the program
may be useless for the program verification. Predicates can be selected
from the failures of a SMT solvers, but they are in the abstract domains
considered by the SMT solver, without guarantee of being inductive. Another way to select the useful basic predicates is to extract them by monitoring program executions [117, 448] (but the problem of defining what
to observe is the same as choosing an abstract domain, and is limited by
this arbitrary choice).

388

27.8

Conclusion

An abstraction of an abstract structural semantics (specified as an
instance of the abstract interpreter) is an abstract structural semantics
(specified as another instance of the abstract interpreter), obtained by
abstraction of the abstract domain. Hence the abstract interpretation
problem is reduced to the abstract interpretation of the primitives of
an abstract domain, and the abstract interpreter can be reused without
needing any other change.
The program verification methods of chapters 25 and 26 for a concrete
structural semantics
ity semantics

¤

S on a concrete domain

on

¤

(e.g., the reachabil-

of chapter 19) are exactly the same for an

abstract structural semantics
S on an abstract domain . But this
abstraction may not simplify the program verification because the existence of an invariant in the abstract domain
may still be undecidable
[711]. Of course one can always simplify the abstract domain but then
the program property of interest can no longer be expressed in the simplified abstract domain. So, the remaining problem with which we cope
in the following chapters is that proofs for iteration statements require
some form of mechanized induction.
The idea of a hierarchy of semantics applies in other scientific domains,
for example, systems biology [304, 358].

Abstract Cartesian Semantics
The view that abstraction consists of replacing concrete values by abstract
values in [572, 741, 899, 967] is restrictive and does not allow, for example,
relational analyses.
Such abstract value-based static analyses can be formalized as a Cartesian
abstraction in which relationships between values of variables are lost.

28.1

Cartesian Semantics

A Cartesian semantics captures the possible values of variables at each
program point but not their relationships. It is named after René
Descartes, a French philosopher, mathematician, and scientist, who developed analytic geometry, using algebra to describe geometry by means
of a coordinate system [315]. Cartesian analyses are called “attribute
independent” in [540, section 12.2].

390

28.1.1

Cartesian Abstraction

The Cartesian abstraction abstracts a relational property expressing a relation between values of variables as a conjunction of properties on the
values of each variable that are unrelated which are independent of the
values of the other variables.
For example, the Cartesian abstraction of property P

28.9

Conclusion

We have designed a collecting semantics for Cartesian abstract interpretation by abstraction of the reachability semantics. Although the given
examples are for finitary abstract domains, this is not mandatory (contrary to the understanding of static analysis in which values are replaced
by symbolic abstract values [572, 741, 899, 967]). Interval analysis [234]
421

is an example of infinitary Cartesian abstraction. Cartesian abstraction is
the basis of SLAM[80], a widely advertised static analyzer of device drivers
lacking precision and scalability. It is also used in Astrée [113] for analyzing control-command software, but in conjunction with many complementary relational scalable abstract domains for precision. Cartesian
abstraction need not be on all dimensions of the abstract domain; an example is [506]. Moreover, the Cartesian abstraction need not necessarily
be on variables. It can be on any finite projection set, for example, on
selected program expressions [919, 920].

29.3

Conclusion

Reductions can improve the precision of analyses. This was shown for
local iterations for tests on Cartesian abstract domains. This is also useful
for type inference. For example, Ada [521] allows for user-defined overloading of predefined arithmetic operators not only on the basis of argument types (as previously done in Algol68 [979]), but also on result types.
So, Bernd Krieg-Brückner designed an iterated reduction algorithm of the
top-down type inference of the result type from the argument types and a
bottom-up type inference of the argument types from the type inference
that was adopted in Ada [521, section 7.5.1, rule 5]. This extends to higherorder types, as in the CASL formal specification language [57].
However, the precision gain for relational domains may not be that spectacular when Boolean operators can be taken into account precisely. This
is why, for example, the Astrée static analyzer [113] does not use local iterations for tests.
Another example of reduction is given in chapter 51, “Reduced Forward—
Backward Analysis.”

Euclidean Division

The Euclidean division of an integer n ℤ by the divisor d ℤ {0} is the
unique pair q, r of a quotient q and rest r such that n = qd + r with 0 r
< |d|. If r = 0 then d divides n (or n is a multiple of d) written d/n.

Congruences

We let c + mℤ {z ℤ | k ℤ . z = c + km} be the congruence class of c
modulo m. This is the set of all integers z equal to c ℤ modulo m ℤ so
that m divides z − c, written m/z − c or z c (mod m). c is called the residue
of z modulo m [398, p. 2].

Canonical Congruences

The same set c + mℤ can be defined by different residues and moduli. For
example, 2 + 4ℤ = 6 + −4ℤ because if z = 2 + 4k then z = 6 + (−4)(1 − k).
A canonical representation is obtained by requiring m 0 and, if m ≠ 0,
by requiring c to be the least residue such that 0 c < m. For example,
c + 1ℤ = ℤ since z ℤ. c ℤ . z = c + 1(z − c) z c (mod 1). The least
residue is 0 with 0 + 1ℤ = ℤ. We use for the empty set which cannot be
represented by a congruence class. In the following we leave implicit that
any congruence we consider has to be normalized into one of ℙ {c + mℤ
| (m = 0) (m > 0 0 c < m)} { }.

30.4

Greatest Common Divisor

The set of common divisors of two integers x and y, not both 0, contains 1
so is not empty and is bounded by |x| by definition of divisibility so the
divisors have a largest/highest element called the greatest common divisor
of x and y. If x = y = 0 then all integers divide them so there is no greatest
divisor. By convention, we define g cd0 0 = 0.
Define the greatest common divisor of two integers, not both 0, as the
largest positive integer which divides both integers.

30.5

Bachet–Bézout Identity

The following theorem is due to Claude-Gaspard Bachet de Méziriac [59,
proposition XVIII] and was generalized by Étienne Bézout [116] to polynomials.

430

Theorem 30.7 (Bachet–Bézout’s identity) let a and b be integers.
There exist (nonunique) Bézout coefficients x, y ℤ such that ax + by = a
gcd b.
Moreover, a gcd b is the smallest positive integer that can be written as ax
+ by. Any integer of the form ax + by is a multiple of the greatest common
divisor a gcd b.
Proof of theorem 30.7 Bézout’s coefficients are not unique, for example 2 × 1 + 4 × 0 = 2 ×−1 + 4 × 1 = 2 × 3 + 4 ×−1 = 2 = 2 gcd 4.
If a = b = 0 then ax + by = a gcd b = 0 gcd 0 = 0 by choosing, for example, x
= y = 0. If a = 0, b ≠ 0 then ax + by = by = 0 gcd b = b by choosing y = 1. It is
the same when b = 0 and a ≠ 0.
Otherwise, a ≠ 0 and b ≠ 0. Let S = {ax + by ℕ+ | x, y ℤ} be the set
of integral positive linear combinations of a and b. |a| S so S is not
empty. Because S ℕ+ , S is well founded, and therefore S has a minimal
element m S. By definition of S, there exists u, v ℤ such that m = au+bv.
By Euclidean division we have a = mq + r where 0 r < m. Assume by
contradiction that r > 0. Then r = a − mq = a − (au + bv)q = a(1 − qu) + b(vq)
> 0 proving that r S (for x = 1 − qu and y = vq) in contradiction to r < m
and m is the minimum of S. So r = 0 proving that m divides a. Similarly m
divides b.
By definition a gcd b is the greatest divisor of both a and b so m a gcd b.
Because a gcd b divides both a and b, it divides au + bv = m so a gcd b m.
By antisymmetry, m = a gcd b.
If i = ax + by > 0 then i S so a gcd b = m i because m is minimal in S,
proving that a gcd b is the smallest positive integer that can be written as
ax + by.
If i = ax + by S then a gcd b divides a and b so divides ax + by = i so i is a
multiple of a gcd b.

Solution to exercise 30.1 Let S = {n − qd ℕ | q ℤ}. This set if not
empty for n 0 and k = 0 or n < 0 and k = −a. Because S ℕ it is well
founded and has a minimum element r. We have r = n − qd 0 for some
q ℤ. Assume by reduction ad absurdum that r d. Then r − d = n − (q +
1)d S in contradiction to the minimality of r S proving r < d.
To prove unicity, assume that n = qd + r and n = q′d + r′ with 0 r, r′ < d.
Then |r − r′| < d. Moreover r′− r = n − q′d − (n − qd) = q(q − q′) so r′− r is a

Cartesian Congruence Analysis
The Cartesian congruence analysis discovers congruence properties x = a
(mod b) of values x ℤ of integer variables x where the integer coefficients
a, b ℕ are automatically inferred by the analysis. It generalizes the constancy analysis x = c (mod 0) of section 28.8.3 and the parity analysis x =
p (mod 2), p {0, 1} of section 28.8.1.

Example of Cartesian Congruence Analysis

Consider the program
where variables are initialized to 0.
Initially x = y = 0 + 0ℤ at ℓ1 and ℓ2 . y = 0 + 0ℤ is even so after execution of
the iteration body x = 0 + 0ℤ or x = 6 + 0ℤ and y = 0 + 0ℤ or y = 1 + 0ℤ at ℓ1 .
It follows that x = 0 + 6ℤ and y = 0 + 1ℤ at ℓ1 hence at ℓ2 because the test x
< 100 provides no congruence information. y = 0 + 1ℤ can be odd or even
at ℓ2 so at ℓ5 we get either x = 3 + 6ℤ in the first case and x = 6 + 6ℤ = 0 +
6ℤ in the second case. Therefore x = 0 + 3ℤ and y = 1 + 1ℤ = 0 + 1ℤ at the
end of the loop body. The join of x = 0 + 6ℤ and x = 0 + 3ℤ at ℓ1 yields x = 0
+ 3ℤ while y = 0 + 1ℤ is stable. One more iteration yields x = 3 + 3ℤ or x =
6 + 3ℤ that is x = 0 + 3ℤ, which is stable. We conclude that x is congruent
to 3 whereas y can be any integer value.

31.11

Conclusion

The Cartesian integer congruence static analysis is due to Philippe
Granger [438], who generalized to rationals [441] and linear congruence
equalities [439]. François Masdupuy introduced interval congruences [a,
b] + mℤ [664] and trapezoidal congruences [663]. Antoine Miné designed
zone congruences [689].
The Cartesian congruence analysis is used in Astrée [113], for example,
to check that data structures are well aligned on word boundaries in computer memory, for example, to multiples of the word size.

Dynamic Interval Analysis
Interval arithmetics in scientific computing was developed by Ramon E.
Moore [715, 716, 717] to put bounds on rounding errors in floating-point
computations [522, 769]. Instead of computing with a floating-point number representing an uncertain real x, the computation is performed with
the two ends of an interval

where x and

are floating-point num-

bers such that
. This is an abstraction of a real trace semantics in
which each real trace is abstracted by one interval trace (which is a property of that real trace) where reals are abstracted by float intervals along
the trace. So, the real computation is replaced by the computation of a
float interval property. Whereas a test on a real takes one or the other alternative, tests on float intervals can take both true and false alternatives.
So the real trace cannot be overapproximated by a single interval trace
only. One must consider a set of interval traces (see section 32.5), each
one being explored in turn, which may lead to combinatorial explosion.

Constants

compilation may introduce an error, that is, overflow with integers
or rounding error for a float that must be taken into account. For
example, the decimal 0.1 is 0.000(1100) in binary so has no exact
binary representation on finitely many bits. It is approximated as
0.10000000149011611938476562500… in single precision.

32.6

On Floating Point Computations

Unfortunately, real computations are usually performed using floatingpoint arithmetics. One computes only one floating-point value hoping it
is not too far from the real one. This problem has been deeply studied
in static analysis [64, 289, 305, 411, 428, 429, 430, 431, 432, 433, 659]. Another dynamic analysis solution is to check the precision with an interval
analysis.
Consider the execution with reals (at least, their semantics), floats and
float intervals, maybe with different possible execution traces for float
intervals due to the nondeterminacy of tests. These interval executions
abstract both the real and float executions.
If there is only one interval execution trace or we can prove that the real
and float executions follow exactly the same control path then the real
473

execution is in the join of the interval executions to which the float execution belongs, when projected on all program points.
Otherwise, the real and float executions may have followed different
paths but both are guaranteed to belong to the union of all interval
executions projected on all program points.
In both cases this provides an estimate of the rounding error of the float
execution compared to the ideal real execution. Of course, the estimate
might be rough because specific properties of the computation are not
taken into account (e.g.„ [524, pp. 91–94]).

32.7

Affine Arithmetic

Interval arithmetic is imprecise. For example, if x [1, 4] then x −x
[1−4, 4−1] = [−3, 3] instead of [0, 0]. The problem as that the arguments
of functions cannot be correlated by a Cartesian abstraction. So we have
to independently take into consideration all possible values of variables
within their interval of variation.
Several solutions have been proposed to solves this imprecision problem
[746]. One of them, affine arithmetics [206, 913], represents an interval
by x = a0 + a1 εx where
,
, and εx [−1, 1] is a fresh
auxiliary variable. Then x − x = (a0 + a1 εx ) − (a0 + a1 εx ) = 0 + 0εx , as required.
In general a program involves several variables so that we have an affine
form x = a0 + a1 ε1 + a2 ε2 + + an εn . This implies x [a0 − d,a0 + d] where
is the total deviation of x. This is, by interval arithmetic, the
smallest interval that contains all possible values of x, assuming that each
εi ranges independently over the interval [−1,+1]. For m variables, the
affine constraints determine a zonotope [679], a center-symmetric convex
polytope in ℝm , whose faces are themselves center symmetric [100, ch. 9].

32.8

Conclusion

Ramon E. Moore [715, 716, 717] may have introduced the first dynamic
program analysis ever to put bounds on rounding (or roundoff) errors in
floating-point computations. As shown in section 32.5, it is an abstract
interpretation of the trace semantics of chapters 6 and 7 so can be computed at runtime for one trace at a time (i.e., during one program execution). Tests may have to consider many executions, which can be quite
inefficient.
Our formalization of the float interval semantics as an abstraction of the
different from the fixreal semantics uses an approximation preorder
point ordering (also called computational ordering). This is a rare exam474

ple of application of theorem 18.21 in abstract interpretation with [248,
737].
Other dynamic analyses have been designed to cope with the imprecision
of floating-point computations. For example, [107, 846] duplicate every
floating-point computation with computations in higher precision to detect discrepancies at runtime. [952] embeds an abstract interpreter into a
runtime execution for verifying numerical accuracy and robustness properties of floating point computations.
Dynamic interval analysis can be extended to ball analysis (also known
as midpoint-radius interval arithmetic) [950, 951].
Dynamic interval analysis is different from other instrumented dynamic
analyses (or runtime verification) [96, 361, 468, 469] in that it does not
collect information upon executions and checks it to verify a specification
but replaces that execution (on reals or floats) by another one (on float
intervals).
We think that these other instrumented dynamic analyses can also be formalized by abstract interpretation of one execution trace. An example
is regular model checking [233] in which executions are monitored by a
regular expression specifying sequences of invariants. Other examples of
runtime analyses are the Firefox’s Javascript JIT compiler integer interval
analysis [149] and the static analyzer of the Extended Berkeley Packet Filter in Linux Kernel [957]. A dynamic analysis can be directly constructed
by considering a single execution at a time, as defined by abstraction to
a transition system (see chapter 42, “Stateful Prefix Trace Semantics”), instead of all possible executions (as in static analysis). [809] formalizes the
coverage and precision of dynamic analysis (on finitely many execution
traces).
Instrumented dynamic analysis consists essentially in checking the abstraction of one execution trace (e.g.„ [631]). The program is instrumented
to generate an event stream. This observed stream is an abstraction of
the execution trace, which is checked by the runtime verifier. The runtime verifier can also be embedded into the observed program to check,
for example, for temporal properties [233, 340].
Static interval analysis cannot be performed at runtime because it must
deal with all possible program computation traces in finite time (it is nevertheless possible to consider only one execution and perform an analysis
of this execution, for example, [759]). We study static interval analysis in
the next chapter 33. It is a Cartesian abstraction of chapter 28 that is an abstraction of the reachability semantics of chapter 19 (itself an abstraction
of the trace semantics of chapters 6 and 7).

Static Interval Analysis
We generalize Cartesian static analyses like sign or constant analysis to
interval analysis (also called range or box analysis) where the value of

numerical variables is bounded by a minimal and a maximal value between which all reachable values of a variable must stand.

which is an abstraction of one maximal execution trace of chapter 7,
range analysis of this chapter 33 is a Cartesian abstraction (developed
in chapter 28) of the reachability analysis of chapter 19 (hence of all
possible execution traces of chapter 7).

33.5

Extrapolation by Widening

The idea of the widening is to extrapolate from an iterate xn and the next
one xn+1 to an upper bound xn xn+1 in order to accelerate or enforce the
convergence of the iterates in finitely many steps. The price to be paid is
a loss of precision, a sound although imprecise answer being considered
better than no answer at all by memory and time resources exhaustion.
In the following example, the derivative is used to accelerate convergence
by extrapolation (as in Newton–Raphson iteration method [524]).

33.8

Modular Interval Analysis

In practice, machines have bounded integers between min_int and
max_int. In case of overflow outside these bounds, the program semantics may specify that execution stops and goes on only when all operations
provide results between these bounds. This is easy to take into account
(provided the abstract operations do not themselves involve overflows)
using − = min_int and = max_int for the widening/narrowing. This
is also easy for floating-point numbers, rounding toward − for the
lower bound and toward + for the upper bound calculation of intervals
[124, 268]. A precise nonrelational abstract domain for floating-point
operations is made by splitting into positive values, negative values,
zeroes, infinities, and NaNs [387].
Another option is modular arithmetic, making it possible for computations to “wrap around” (e.g., min_int-1 = max_int) which must be handled
soundly in the interval abstract domain [389, 732, 884, 891].

488

33.10

Zonotopic Abstraction

In the same way that zonotopes have been used to improve the precision
of dynamic interval arithmetics in scientific computing (see section 32.7),
they have also been used to improve the precision of static interval reachability analysis of programs [411, 429, 433] and hybrid systems [432, 593].

33.11

Conclusion

Intervals were the first non-Noetherian abstract domain thus requiring
iteration extrapolation operators for convergence acceleration [234, 235].
Some programming languages such as Pascal [986] and its followers have
interval types. The compiler uses a simple type inference with an integer
base type and the bounds are checked at runtime. Most of these checks
can be eliminated at compile-time by a static interval analysis. The same
observation applies to runtime array-bound checking.
Although the basic abstract operations are the same, static interval analysis should not be confused with the runtime interval analysis of chapter
32 used in numerical analysis to cope with rounding errors of floats [715].
Of course, this dynamic/runtime interval arithmetic abstract interpretation of program executions can be overapproximated by a static/compiletime one to statically analyze programs manipulating floating-point numbers [428, 525, 659].
An interval analysis is used in [482] to detect unseen inputs of neural networks as novel to avoid missclassification. The interval abstract domain
is used in [58, 963] to show that for any function f, there exists a neural network whose abstract interpretation is an arbitrarily close approximation
of the collecting semantics of f.
In addition to the zonotopes of section 33.10, various refinements of interval analysis have been studied, such as symbolic intervals [745, 853];
489

interval congruences [664]; anti-intervals (to close the domain by complement with [− , ], as used by the PolySpace Verifier [317]); by lists of
intervals such as [− ,1000], [1002, ] or boxes [451] (union of disjoint intervals encoded by a propositional formula over interval constraints and
represented by Linear Decision Diagrams [169], an extension of Binary
Decision Diagrams [150]); by symbolic bounds [992]; and more generally
by relational domains. The relative precision of different numerical abstract domains with respect to the interval domain is studied in [37].
1. 1. This is the confusion made by [474] in claiming that the abstract
domain is infinite but requires no widening thanks to a constraint
resolution algorithm. In fact, the abstract domain is finite for a given
program and it becomes infinite only when considering all possible
programs. Moreover, for a given program, the constraint resolution
algorithm is a least fixpoint iteration in an abstract domain satisfying the ascending condition [251], so without surprise, no widening
is necessary [251].

X
EFFECTIVE FIXPOINT APPROXIMATION
A static analyzer is an instance of the abstract interpreter that automatically infers in inductive program property in a given abstract domain .
The main challenge is to compute the limit of iterates for fixpoints.
Convergence acceleration techniques ensures that can be done in finite
time up to a loss of precision but not a loss of soundness (chapter 34).
In checking a specification, this specification can be used to improve the
precision of the fixpoint approximation (chapter 35).
The reduced product is a useful technique to decompose the design of the
abstract domain
into parts to get a modular and extensible abstract
interpreter (chapter 36).

490

34
Fixpoint Approximation by Extrapolation and
Interpolation
The fixpoint approximation by extrapolation with widening and interpolation by narrowing that we illustrated in chapter 33 for intervals can be
generalized to any analysis in a non-Noetherian abstract domain (i.e., not
satisfying the ascending (dually descending) chain condition (ACC/DCC)
that every infinite increasing (decreasing) chain is finite).

34.3

Non-increasing Abstract Iteration Transformers

When considering nested loops, the transformer
in
(21.11) of the outer loop does depend on the approximation of the fixpoint semantics of the inner loop using theorem 34.6, which, because the
widening is not increasing, may itself be nonincreasing. Therefore in theorem 34.6, the abstract transformer
cannot be assumed to be increasing. Soundness relies only on the increasingness of the concrete transformer f, which is always the case because, intuitively, more possible in496

teractions with the execution environments yield more possible program
executions.

34.6

Delayed Widening

In theorem 34.6 the iteration with terminating widening applies the same
widening at each iteration step. More generally, the widening
may
depend on the iteration step n. For example, the widening may become
coarser over time n. An example is delayed widening [124], which is the
join for the k iterates after entering the loop, or after a new path has
been explored in a loop [124, 268]. The further iterates use to enforce
termination.

34.9
Upward Iteration with Widening Refined by a
Downward Iteration with Narrowing
In practice a concrete fixpoint is first abstracted in an abstract fixpoint,
the upward iterates are accelerated by extrapolation with widening and
next refined by downward iterates accelerated by interpolation with narrowing.
For an increasing abstract transformer , the downward iterates accelerated by interpolation with narrowing converge to a fixpoint without

501

Figure 780:
jumping over any of them. Therefore, the information lost by the widening may not always be recovered by the narrowing. If the upward widening iteration jumps over a fixpoint which is not the least one, then the
downward narrowing is blocked by this fixpoint.
Further improvements are considered in [231, 455].

34.10

Chaotic and Asynchronous Iterations

Because the abstract interpreter of chapter 21 proceeds by structural induction, the widening needs to be done only once at the head of loops.
With unstructured abstract interpreters based on the equational semantics of chapter 23, the static analysis is specified by a system of equations

Figure 781:
that can be solved by the chaotic iterations of chapter 22 (where at each
iteration an arbitrary nonempty subset of the equations evolves) or asynchronous iterations (the equations evolve in parallel) with fairness hypotheses (no equation is delayed forever and the result of any equation
evolution is eventually available to all equations) [220, 236]. A dependency analysis of the equations can be used to identify cycles that must
be broken by a widening [221, ch. 4]. Good iterations strategies should ensure rapid convergence by avoiding useless repetitions of computations
and loss of precision [138].

502

34.11

Finitary Versus Infinitary Abstractions

Following an argument of [246], an interval analysis with widening/narrowing will always terminate and so can explore only a finite part
of the lattice of intervals. For example, for program P1001 = while (x < n)x
= x+1 ;, this is and even the smaller part on the right when it is using a
widening with threshold 1001. A static analysis with these finite domains
would find the same result for program P1001 . This is not an argument
in favor of using only abstractions in finite domains (or in Noetherian
domains, that is, domains with no infinite strictly increasing chains).

Figure 782:
• Using a single Noetherian abstract domain for all programs will fail
on infinitely many programs where the widening/narrowing analysis will succeed. Consider for example the family of programs

Figure 783:
where n 0 is an integer constant. The interval analysis examplified
in sections 33.5 and 33.6 for n = 1001 will always yield the loop
invariant [0,n] for any particular n
ℕ. These invariants form
an infinite strictly increasing chain of intervals. Any Noetherian
abstract domain will not be able to represent infinitely many of
these invariants. Therefore an analysis using a Noetherian domain
will fail on infinitely many programs where the analysis with
widening/narrowing succeeds.

503

• Finding the adequate domain for each particular program amounts
to doing a pre-analysis (globally or at each iteration step) of this particular program to discover the necessary invariants to be included
in the abstract domain. However to determine these useful invariants (or a finite superset) the pre-analysis must know the result of
the analysis, so this solution is circular.

34.12

Hidden Widenings and Narrowings

As noticed in [251, section 6.2], a solution to the convergence problem is
to mask the explicit use of a widening

in the iterations of

by iterating

.
This is, for example, the case in the Robin Milner polymorphic typing algorithm [685], which involves a hidden widening to handle recursion and
can be potentially improved [224].
Another example is [11] in the abstract domain of first-order formulas
where, for example, i. (0 i < n) (xi+1 = xi + 1) is widened to i. xi = x0 +
i.
A narrowing can be hidden by choosing x Δ y = y, which is sound by theorem 34.16 and termination enforced by stopping the downwards iterations after an arbitrary number of iterates.
When restricted to specific classes of programs, such as non-nested simple loops, guarded by a linear condition on integer variables and consisting of incrementations/decrementations of these variables, the limit of
the fixpoint iterations can be computed exactly as a Presburger formula
(first-order theory of the natural numbers with addition and equality only,
without multiplication). So the widening can deliver exact results, at a
high complexity cost (e.g.„ doubly exponential). The restrictions and costs
limit the applicability of the method [207, 989].

34.13

Duality

Widenings and narrowings are not dual but have duals that can be used
to approximate fixpoints iteratively with convergence acceleration, as follows:
and shown on figure 34.18.
An example of dual narrowing is Graig interpolation [677] in the abstract
domain of first-order formulas (this is not a widening [231, 678] and it
does not enforce termination).

Figure 784:

Figure 785: Figure 34.18Inductive and coinductive fixpoint iterations

505

34.14

Conclusion

We have assumed upper continuous functions but the results extend to
increasing functions using transfinite iterations [221, ch. 4].
Widening and narrowing were introduced in [234], and their duals in
[235]. [221] distinguishes between extrapolating and terminating widening/narrows and duals because these hypotheses are independent; see
also [392].
Terminating widenings are not increasing and cannot be increasing, as
shown in section 34.2. Therefore fixpoints might not exist but soundness
can be established with respect to an increasing concrete semantics with
fixpoint existence guarantee.
The fact that widenings are not increasing and cannot be increasing if
termination of infinite iterations is to be ensured is often misunderstood.
An example, among others, is [705, ch. 5]. Interval analysis is considered
as an instance of the so-called “monotone data flow analysis framework”
[553] assuming that transformers are increasing, which is not the case of
widening. The widening is therefore introduced in a framework assuming hypotheses that exclude it, so conclusions are simply wrong.
Widening and narrowing were the central idea for scalability of static
analysis. They do not fit in previous data-flow analysis frameworks
requiring finitary domains and monotonicity [27, 553, 572, 967], which
severely limits their expressive power (section 34.11 and [246]).
Some fixpoint solvers such as TD [875] incorporate widenings and narrowings to cope with non-Noetherian abstract domains.
More general results on widenings, narrowings, and their duals are provided in [231]. Widenings and narrowing will not improve a fixpoint.
This can be done by perturbation of the fixpoint, analysis of the iterations to identify losses of information, restarting increasing and decreasing sequences from well-chosen iterates, and other methods [141]. [39,
45] proposed to interwind widening and narrowing during iteration. Extrapolation and interpolation operators can be designed by analysis of the
fixpoint iterations [278].
So-called acceleration techniques identify those fixpoint equations on
those abstract domains for which an exact solution can be computed
directly [425, 426]. Policy iteration applies to those fixpoints of increasing
functions F which is a combination of “simpler” increasing functions g,
for which there are fast algorithms to compute their least fixpoints [9,
216, 400, 401, 404, 405, 406, 874]. [559] combines iterations and, locally,
policy iteration.

506

35
Fixpoint Checking
Many static analyses are performed to check properties of program components S. This frequently amounts to proving that lfp ℱ S
P where
property P is a specification. A common solution based on the fixpoint induction theorem 24.1 consists of computing an inductive property I that
is shown to be invariant ℱ S (I) I so that lfp ℱ S
I and stronger
than P, that is, I P.
A better solution is to use the specification P to improve the precision of
the invariant I. The invariant I is inferred assuming the specification P
does hold. Then the invariant I is checked to imply that lfp ℱ S
P.

35.3

Abstract Invariants May Not Help Enough

Theorem 35.1 shows that adding information about the program behavior can only help the analysis. Therefore if a static analysis is not precise enough, for example, because of excessive extrapolations or interpolations, adding a specification of what the static analyzer should infer is
sound and can only help.
509

Figure 789:
However, this may be insufficient in general. The main reason is that if the
specification P is given in the concrete then it will be abstracted in P in the
abstract domain, where the concrete information may be lost. Moreover,
if the specification P is given in the abstract then it might not be inductive.

35.4

Conclusion

Astrée [113] is based on theorem 35.5. In a first phase, the static analysis
is done assuming the specification holds. Then, in a second phase, it is
verified that the specification does hold.

[226] considers equivalent forms of theorems 35.1 and 35.5 based on duality. [232] introduces other induction principles for proving properties
of fixpoints.

36
Reduced Product
The direct product of several static analyses is the conjunction of the separately computed analyses. The reduced product of several static analyses
[241] computes in the conjunction of their abstract domains. In that case,
information on program executions captured by one domain can be used
to improve the precision of the information provided by other abstract domains. This is called a meaning-preserving reduction. As shown in chapter
29, reductions can be iterated to obtain more precise and still sound analyses.

36.1

Direct Product

The direct product of abstract domains can be used to perform simultaneous independent analyses of a program. The set of properties of the
direct product is the Cartesian product of the component abstract properties, the concretization is the conjunction (meet) of the concretizations
for each abstract domain, and the transformers are performed componentwise without interactions.

36.4

Iterated Pairwise Reduction

36.4.1

Pairwise Reduction

The strong reduction operators
of theorem 36.19 and
of theorem
36.24 may be difficult to compute algorithmically because they involve
all abstract domains of the direct product. In adding a new abstract domain to increase precision of the analysis, the strong reduction between
all domains must be completely redesigned.
For simplicity, weaker reductions are useful. Pairwise reduction is an
example of such a weak meaning-preserving of the direct product reduction. It applies between two abstract domains only and leaves the other
domains unchanged. When a new abstract domain is added to the product of abstract domains of an abstract interpreter, one need only to design
a pairwise reductions between the new abstract domain and (some of) the
existing ones.
Several weak reductions can be strengthen by iteration. This provides a
general algorithm for constructing/approximating reduced products by
iterated pairwise reductions, which can be implemented once for all in
the static analyzer/verifier.

Example 36.32 (Nelson-Oppen algorithm) The satisfiability modulo
theories (SMT) problem is a decision problem for logical formulas with
respect to combinations of background theories expressed in classic firstorder logic with equality. The Nelson-Oppen algorithm [748] combines
decision procedures for these background theories. It is an iterated pairwise reduction [275]. The reduction consists of propagating the equalities
and inequalities between variables derived from one theory to all other
theories. This is incomplete. For example, assume that a theory of signs
derives x 0 and a theory of parity deriving that x is odd. None derives
x ≠ 0 because this is not an inequality between variables. Hence x 0 is
not reduced to x > 0. Completeness can be obtained by putting restrictions on the background theories, for example, that they do not share
symbols. Hence we cannot have both sign and parity background theo525

ries that share +, −, and so forth. Such restrictions to ensure completeness
are meaningless in program verification using SMT solvers because program verification and analysis are, by Rice’s theorem 9.12, undecidable
anyway.

36.4.5

Widening

The widening/narrowing [235] of a reduced product is often defined
componentwise using widenings/narrowings of the component abstract
domains. This ensures convergence for the product. However, it must
be proved that the reduction does not break down the termination of
the product widening, in which case reduction must be weakened or the
widening strengthened [215].
Example 36.39 The closure operation in the zone abstract domain of
chapter 40 can be considered a reduction between separate domains,
each considering only a pair of variables: if one applies the classic widening operation on zones followed by closure (reduction), then termination
is no longer ensured as shown in section 40.1.8 (the same holds for the
octagon abstract domain; see [692, fig. 25–26]).
36.4.6
tion

Practical Implementation of the Iterated Pairwise Reduc-

Abstract interpreters are often built incrementally, by successively adding
new abstract domains and combining them with already existing ones by
pairwise iterated reduction.
In order to avoid modifying existing domains each time a new one is introduced, one can use a common interface
, called a communication
channel [178, 267], between abstract domains. The communication channel represents the information shared between the abstract domains of
the reduced product, as defined by a concretization
. Then
abstract domains ℙi are enriched with two primitive operations.
is used to communicate information of abstract
send
domain ℙi to the other abstract domains involved in the reduced product,
through the communication channel. For soundness, it must satisfy
(send(P, Q)).
receive
is used to receive information from the other
abstract domains, through the communication channel, to improve
the information encoded by the abstract domain ℙi . It must satisfy

.
i

The abstract domain ℙ uses the received information to improve the precision of its operations i , i , i , i , assigni x, A , testi B , and testi B .

529

These operations may have to be adjusted when introducing a new abstract domain that may help improve their precision.
For example 36.32, the communication channel is equalities and disequalities between variables. For the reduced product of sign and parity in
exercise 36.4, the communication channel can be equalities and disequalities between a variable and a constant. By asking the question x ≠ 0?,
the sign abstract domain can improve x 0 to x < 0, x 0 to x > 0, x = 0 to
, and so on. This question can be answered, for example, by the parity
abstract domain (when the parity of the variable and the constant differ),
the constant abstract domain (when the variable is equal to a different
constant), and so forth.
Finally, a scheduler is in charge of orchestrating the reduction communications during the fixpoint computation. It must be extended, for each
new abstract domain introduced in the reduced product, to decide which
meaningful communications have to be performed, and in which order.
Only a number of the possible pairwise reductions of definition 36.25 may
be performed, maybe in a given order specified by the scheduler [125, 214,
267, 546]. For cost saving, the reduction in definition 36.29 need not be
iterated until reaching a fixpoint. It can be stopped at any time.
Many verification methods and static analyzers use auxiliary/intermediate/ghost
variables. They are used to memoize the abstract value of a function of
the program semantics. This can be done at some time in the computation, such as the auxiliary variables used to record the initial value of
variables in the relational reachability semantics of section 19.1.2. More
generally, this can be a value that changes during the computation (such
as the value of an expression). Whereas the value of program variables
are modified explicitly though an assignment (maybe indirectly through
pointers), ghost variables are modified implicitly when the quantities
upon which they depend are modified. This may be problematic in a
reduced product because an abstract domain modifying a ghost variable
must inform the other abstract domains. An elegant solution to this
problem, extending the expressiveness of the reduced product and the
way abstract interpreters are designed, is proposed by [179] and [178,
part IV].

36.5

Conclusion

More properties of reduced products are studied in [274]. (It is also shown
that the Nelson-Oppen combinations of theories [748] used in satisfiability
modulo theories (SMT) solvers is a reduced product of abstract domains.)
[1002] defines the reduced product of abstract domains for constraintsolving.
The reduced product and its variants are essential for extending static an530

alyzers by introducing new abstractions without having to redo the whole
static analyzer [267]. Some static analyzers with a monolithic design, such
as Infer [162] and more generally type inference [224] lack this capacity
of being simply extensible.
Because the full fixpoint iterated reduction of the reduced product may
be costly, partial reductions are cheaper and often preferred in practice.
There are many possible variants, with many different names, which are
mostly variants for specific partial reductions [198, 211, 372, 449, 626].
The decision of where, when, and in which order to do reductions given
in chapter 29 or this chapter is a question of balance between the admissible cost and desired precision of the analysis. This is often a matter
of experimentation starting with minimal reductions and adding those
indispensable for precision. See, for example, [267] which proposes an
extensible implementation of reduction to facilitate the inclusion of new
abstract domains through a common interface.
As mentioned in section 36.4.6, [179] extends the reduced product to allow
for abstract domains to record information about the history of computation using ghost variables. Other compositions of abstract domains have
been proposed in [36, 213, 241, 415, 418, 547]. In particular, disjunctive
combinations of abstract domains allow for a case analysis based on program control [174] or values of variables [273] or for an arbitrary one,
when considering all possible disjunctions [241, 370] with various widening strategies [66, 67, 330, 331, 451].
The inverse problem of composing abstract domains is that of decomposition into simpler ones; see for example, [213] for the reduced product
inverse and [852] for tree decompositions to define an abstract domain.

XI
RELATIONAL STATIC ANALYSIS
A static analysis is relational when the inferred properties do relate the
values of variables.
We provide two examples.
The linear equality analysis (chapter 38) is based on basic mathematical
concepts of linear algebra (chapter 37).
The zone and octagon inequality analyses (chapter 40) are based on basic
mathematical concepts of graphs (chapter 39).

37.4

Solving a System of Linear Equations

A system of linear equations A = may have 0, 1, or many solutions. The
Gauss–Jordan elimination algorithm can be used to effectively compute
them.
37.4.1

Basic Row Transformations

The system A = is augmented to (A| ) by adding the extra column
and putting in reduced row echelon form by Gauss–Jordan elimination,

Figure 830:
540

with three basic row transformations:
• 1. the swap of two rows,
• 2. the multiplication of a row by a nonzero scalar a
{0}, and
• 3. addition of a multiple of one row to another different row.
These basic row transformations of (A | ) do not change the solutions to
A = .
37.4.2

Row Echelon Form

Carl Friedrich Gauss [399, pp. 21–25] showed that by successive applications of the basic row transformations, any augmented matrix can be
transformed in (nonunique) row echelon form. A matrix is in row echelon
form if and only if
• all nonzero rows (rows with at least one nonzero element) are above
any rows of all zeros (so all zero rows, if any, belong at the bottom of the
matrix), and
• the leading coefficient (the first nonzero number from the left, also
called the pivot) of a nonzero row is always equal to 1 and strictly to the
right of the leading coefficient of the row above it.
These two conditions imply that all entries in a column below a pivot are
zeros.

Reduced Row Echelon Form

Wilhelm Jordan [543, pp. 62–83] showed that by successive applications of
the basic row transformations, the augmented matrix can be transformed
in a unique reduced row echelon form. A matrix is in reduced row echelon
form if and only if it is in row echelon form and for each column vector
containing a pivot, this pivot is the only nonzero element in the column.
Example 37.4 is not in reduced form, but

is obtained directly without needing a final backward substitution. More
importantly (and unlike the row echelon form), the reduced row echelon
form of a matrix is unique so provides a canonical form.

Assume that A(n × m) is the augmented matrix with n rows and m columns.
After the (i − 1)th-step (i = 0,…,n − 1), the Gauss–Jordan elimination algorithm [34] transforms the matrix A in the following form
where the pivots are 1 and unique nonzero elements in their column, and
* represents an arbitrary value. The ith-step is the following [524, p. 50]:

• 1. Find the first column j containing a nonzero element at row k, at
or below row i. If no such j exists, the bottom right of the matrix is
0 and we are done.
• 2. If k ≠ i, exchange rows k and i so that the pivot at A(i, j) is nonzero.
• 3. Set the pivot to 1 by dividing line i by A(i, j).
• 4. Set the column j above and below the pivot to 0 by updating each
row A(ℓ, k), ℓ

Conclusion

Finite dimensional linear algebra and matrix theory pervade mathematics and other sciences.
Considering variable properties, that is, sets of environments as sets of
points, it is possible to abstract them to affine spaces, which yields the
linear equality static analysis of programs of chapter 38.

for y. The linear equality analysis aims at discovering linear equality relations A × =

between values

of the program variables where A and

are inferred by the static analysis. In this example, 2x − y = 0, so x 10
implies y 20. Linear equality analysis was introduced by Michael Karr
[560].

Abstraction of an Expression into an Affine Expression

The program assignments x = A ; in section 4.1 are not necessarily in affine
form. Therefore we use the following affine abstraction of the arithmetic
expression A in section 3.4. The idea is that for nonlinear expressions like
x * y, the static analysis may have determined that the value of x is a scalar
c, so we can use the linear form c.y.
If the abstraction returns then the assignment is handled by lemma
37.19 for eliminating the assigned variable. Otherwise the coefficients
of the variables are summed up to get a linear assignment of section 38.4.

38.7

Conclusion

Michael Karr [560] represents affine spaces as the solution set of linear
equation systems A = represented by the matrix (A | ) (the number
of affine relations between values of variables will be small hence the
dimension of the affine space and the size of the system of generators
will be large). He had to design an original algorithm for the join . A
simpler and more efficient algorithm is proposed by [695, section 5.2.2].
Following what is traditionally done for polyhedral analysis [279],
Markus Müller-Olm and Helmut Seidl [729] introduced the use of systems of generators [729, 730]. [348, 885] studied variations on matrix
representations of affine domains. Integers can be analyzed using
rationals with a concretization in the integers. A better solution is to

562

generalize affine equalities to affine congruences [439]. Other generalizations include modular arithmetics [348] and interval [176] or polynomial
equalities [160, 515, 531, 576, 642, 727, 840, 856, 998].

equality abstract domains.

Graphs
The Roy–Floyd–Warshall algorithm [375, 844, 965] finds shortest paths in
a weighted graph (with no cycle with strictly negative weight). It is an
abstract interpretation of a fixpoint path-finding algorithm. References
[109, 165, 318, 860] are introductions to graph theory.

Graphs

A (directed) graph or digraph G = V, E is a pair of a set V of vertices (or
nodes or points) and a set E ℘(V × V ) of edges (or arcs). A (directed)
edge x, y
V has origin x and end y collectively called extremities (so
the graphs that we consider are always directed). Therefore E is a binary
relation of section 2.2.2 on V. Conversely, a binary relation can be understood as a graph on its field [860]. A graph is finite when the set of V of
vertices (hence E) is finite.

simple paths that overapproximate paths with no cycles (called elementary paths). Let us design the Roy-Floyd-Warshall algorithm by calculus.

39.12

Elementary Paths and Cycles

A cycle is elementary if and only if it contains no internal subcycle (i.e.,
subpath which is a cycle). A path is elementary if and only if it contains no
subpath that is an internal cycle (so an elementary cycle is an elementary
path). The only vertices that can occur twice in an elementary path are
its extremities, in which case it is an elementary cycle.
Example 39.19 In example 39.1, xyz and xz are elementary paths (zz is
a path of length 1). The path xyx is an elementary cycle (zz is a cycle of
length 1). The paths xyzz and xyxyxz and the cycles yxyxy and zzz are not
elementary. We do not consider infinite paths such as xyxyx….

39.17 Calculational Design of the Roy-Floyd-Warshall
Shortest Path Algorithm
The shortest path algorithm of Bernard Roy [844, 845], Bob Floyd [375],
and Steve Warshall [965] for finite graphs is based on the assumption that
the graph has no cycles with strictly negative weights, that is, x V . π
p(x, x) . ω(π) 0. In that case the shortest paths are all elementary because adding a cycle of weight 0 leaves the distance unchanged whereas
a cycle of positive weight would strictly increase the distance on the path.
Otherwise, as shown by example 39.16, if the graph has cycle with strictly
negative weights, the convergence between two vertices containing a cycle with strictly negative weights is infinite to the limit − .
Algorithm 39.30 (Roy-Floyd-Warshall algorithm overapproximating the elementary paths of a finite graph) Let G = V, E be a graph

The essential consequence is that we do not have to consider all paths as
in theorem 39.10 but instead we can consider any subset provided that it
contains all elementary paths. Therefore we can base the design of the
shortest path algorithm on corollary 39.28. Observe that, although p may
contain paths that are not elementary, d is precisely the minimal path
lengths and not some strict overapproximation because
• p contains all elementary paths (so nonelementary paths are longer
than the elementary path between their extremities), and
• no arc has a strictly negative weight (so path lengths are always positive and therefore the elementary paths are the shortest ones).
