49.8

Monomorphic Static Typing

Monomorphic static typing checks statically, at compile time, that evaluation of an expression E will never return a static error Ωσ . This does
not necessarily prevent dynamic errors Ωδ that can be detected only at
runtime (or by more sophisticated static analyses).

49.8.9

Soundness: Typable Expressions Cannot Go Wrong

An expression E is typable if and only if there exists a type judgment Γ Eμ.
Typable expressions cannot go wrong because the execution of a typable
expression cannot produce a static error (but it can produce a dynamic
one such as hd([])).
A typable expression cannot go wrong in that its evaluation never returns
a static error Ωσ .
Lemma 49.19 (typable expressions cannot go wrong) If Γ Eμ then ρ

Notice that go wrong means evaluate to a static error Ωσ , which does not
exclude evaluating to a dynamic error Ωδ .
Proof of lemma 49.19

Figure 1336:

Notice that we have proved type soundness in lemma 49.19 by considering the semantics of types only. This is to be contrasted with the classic
approach [796, section 8.3], which proceeds by induction on a derivation
of the type μ of E according to type inference rules that have to be guessed
a priori. In contrast, we use the semantic interpretation γ of types to
later design the type inference rules in figure 49.41 by calculus (in section
49.9.3), which are then sound by construction.

49.9

Monomorphic Static Type Inference Algorithm

The typing rules section 49.8.13 in Alonso Church style are not algorithmic
because types are sets that may be infinite (e.g., τ hd([]) = Θ in example
49.24). Roger Hindley [499] proposed to finitely represent these infinite
sets by type schemes, that is, monomorphic types with variables. This is
an abstract interpretation based on the symbolic term abstract domain
of chapter 48. This abstraction is in general imprecise. However, due to

830

restrictions on monomorphic types and the considered language, the abstraction turned out to be exact for the sets involved in the typing rules
of section 49.8.13 [224]. This exactness is obtained by restrictions on the
types (e.g., there is no union of types like Boolean or integer, list elements
must all be of the same type, and others) and the programming language
(e.g., the type of branches in a conditional must be the same, and all recursive calls of a procedure must have the same type).
49.9.1

of monotypes.

Figure 1358:
In general, there is a loss of information, for example,
(where = ( int, bool )). However the expressions and the typing rules
have been designed so that there is no expression with type {int, bool}

common generalization abstraction of the set of monotypes of an expression is a monotype with variables that exactly abstracts this set.
Therefore the loss of information is only for the set of monotypes that
are the set of types for no expression.

Conclusion

Pairs and lists date back to John McCarthy’s LISP programming language
[673]. Roger Hindley [500] showed how to infer Alonzo Church monotypes for the λ-calculus [185] using type variables and unification. This
inspired Robin Milner to design a polymorphic type inference algorithm
(so-called algorithm W) in which type variables denotes any fixed but unknown type [685]. The type system was later presented by a structural
deductive system [286] that was proved equivalent to the type inference
algorithm. This initial work gave rise to numerous refinements [796, 797].
Empirical design of types systems leads to errors, for example, [40].
Generalizing monotypes with variables to represent sets of monotypes,
[450] introduced abstract types, which stand for (infinitely) many
monomorphic instances, at different levels of abstraction.
The understanding of type theory as an abstract interpretation is from
[224, 237]. This yields language-independent concepts that apply equally
well, for example, to denotational semantics or resolution-based languages [270]. The classic type theory [796, 797] has difficulties with
modern typing systems taking data values into account that are easily
solved by abstract interpretation. For example, [784] proves the soundness of liquid types [842] (i.e., types refined by abstract properties in a
finite abstract domain) by abstract interpretation. [395] is an example of
a gradual type system designed by abstract interpretation that has been
fully mechanized [292]. Beyond types, types and effects (describing code
side effects [641]) can also be formalized by abstract interpretation [385,
961]. [386] shows that this may be useful to catch and fix soundness
errors in postulated types and effects systems.

XIII
BACKWARD STATIC ANALYSIS
A forward/deductive static analysis computes states reachable from specified initial states of the computation (chapters 19 and 20).
Inversely, a backward/abductive static analysis computes initial states
from states specified to be reachable by the computation (chapter 50).
A forward/backward static analysis computes states reachable from specified initial states and reaching specified states of the computation. This
is called a reduced forward/backward analysis when it involves the iteration of successive forward and backward analyses (chapter 51).

50
Backward Accessibility Semantics
It is often useful to reason on program executions backward, in reverse
execution order, as shown by Dijkstra’s weakest (liberal) preconditions
840

Figure 1369:

841

[327] (see section 12.4). For example, for the property x = y to hold at a
program point ℓ2 of program ℓ0 y = 1 ; ℓ1 x = x-y ; ℓ2 , it is necessary and
sufficient that property x = 2 × y did hold at the previous point ℓ1 in the
execution and so that x = 2 did hold at the previous point ℓ0 . Such reasonings can be based on backward/abductive accessibility semantics and are
also called abductive (infer a to explain b) [412] as opposed to forward
reachability semantics, also called deductive (infer b as a consequence of
a). An application of backward analysis is the inference of conditions on
inputs to avoid an error.1
The impossible failure accessibility semantics is the adjoint of the reachability semantics. It specifies a condition on the initial states for reaching
only states satisfying a given reachability condition. This is similar to
(12.11).
The possible success accessibility semantics is the conjugate of the impossible failure accessibility semantics. It specifies a condition on the initial
states for the existence of an execution reaching a state satisfying a given
reachability condition. This is similar to pre (12.).

Conclusion

The backward possible success accessibility semantics
of a program component S is from [221, 222, 241] in which it was derived from
the forward reachability semantics by inversion of the transition system
i.e.
. In this
chapter, the calculational design of the structural backward impossible
was by direct inversion of the

failure accessibility semantics

structural forward reachability semantics
866

, and the backward pos-

sible success accessibility semantics
followed by complement
duality. The two backward semantics can be applied to other languages
(e.g.„ [513]) and conjuncted (e.g.„ [71]). [577] compares the expressive
power of forward and backward static analyses for logic programs.
The same way that the forward reachability semantics of chapter 19 was
the basis for a forward abstract interpreter (chapter 21) leading to forward analyses and forward invariance proof methods (chapter 25), the
backward accessibility semantics of this chapter 50 can be further abstracted to get a backward abstract interpreter ([dual] adjoint to section
21.2), which is the basis for invariance proof methods (such as subgoal induction [721]; see [243, 427]) and automatic static program analysis methods (such as tracing imprecise analysis values back to origin of the imprecision [623]).
Although corollary 50.2 and theorem 50.23 express equivalences between
semantics, this may no longer be true in the abstract. Forward and backward analyses are in general different (e.g.„ [700]) and can be combined
as shown in the next chapter 51. These analyses can be used to check
temporal properties by abstract interpretation; see [256, 665, 666, 667]
and the next chapter 51.
[550] is an example of backward analysis in which verification conditions
are expressed using Horn clauses [511]. Backward analyses are essential
for inferring and proving necessary conditions for program termination,
absence of errors, and sufficient correctness conditions [230, 263, 940,
943]; existential temporal properties [217, 942, 944, 948]; tracing alarms
to their origin [311, 369]; and responsibility analysis [310, 311].

51.5

Conclusion

The combination of forward (reachability/deductive/top-down for
logic/constraint languages) and backward (accessibility/abductive/bottomup) static analyses in sections 51.1 and 51.2, iterated extremal reduction
in section 51.3, and intermediate reduction in section 51.4 have increasing precisions and costs. A reduction is more precise but may be too
costly (a compromise is to reduce at loop head only). The reduction
may also produce slight improvements only with very precise extremal
878

Figure 1456:
analyses. [930] is an example of forward/backward interval analysis
of floating-point numbers augmented by a precision to determine the
minimal accuracy on the inputs and on the intermediary results of a
program containing floating-point computations in order to ensure the
desired accuracy of the outputs.
[332] combines a forward analysis with both impossible failure and possible success backward analyses.
Iterated forward—backward reduction analysis was introduced by [221,
section 5.7.5, pp. (5)-53—(5)-56] and [557]; see [253, section 4] and [256].
They apply to languages such as Prolog [244]. [549] is an example of
backward—forward static analysis with iterated extremal reduction
where verification conditions are expressed with Horn clauses [511]. [72]
noticed that this is less precise than the original iterated intermediate
reduction and proposed a formulation of the intermediate reduction
using Horn clauses. Generalizations to the abstraction of temporal trace
properties are proposed by [665–667].
The iterated forward—backward analysis is the basis for combining program analysis with model checking [252, 253] and, associated with other
test generation techniques, for providing counterexamples to failed specifications [994, 995].

52.1

Soundness by Calculational Design

Soundness of verification or static analysis methods states that proved
or inferred program properties cannot be contradicted by any program
execution as defined by the program semantics. Abstract interpretation
does not keep this notion in the vagueness of informal explanations [638]
but provides a rigorous definition, which is recalled and discussed below.
Formal reasonings on programs P of a language ℙ are reasonings on their
semantics P
providing a formal model of all possible program executions as an element of the semantic domain . The semantic domain
can be chosen at various levels of abstraction as shown in chapters 6, 7, 19,
23, 25, 26, 28, and 42. Program properties are sets of possible semantics
in ℙ ℘( ) (chapter 8). The collecting semantics { P } is the strongest
semantic property of program P (see section 3.10 and chapter 8).
In general, one is interested in a subset of the program properties encoded in a domain ℙ whose meaning is given by a concretization function

. The implication on ℘( ) is on so that γ is increasing. If any property in ℘( ) has a best/ -most precise approximation in
then there is a Galois connection

which is sound if { P } γ( P ) i.e.

P is defined by structural induction on the
grammatical structure of the program P, using fixpoints for iterative or recursive constructs (e.g., chapters 17 and 19), so that the abstract semantics
P can be designed by calculus using induction and fixpoint abstraction
theorems (chapters 16 and 24). Another essential idea is the decomposition of the abstract properties of interest into abstract domains, which
can be verified independently, and assembled inductively via functors
(like the reduced product of chapter 36). This modularity is essential to
scalability [268] and verifiability [563, 564].

52.2

Verification Versus Static Analysis

For either verification or static analysis automation, further abstractions
may be needed to get computer-representable properties (chapter 27).
In both cases, a property has to be discovered and proved to be inductive
(using either structural and/or fixpoint induction). By Rice’s theorem 9.12,
the collecting, as well as the abstract semantics, hence the necessary inductive property are in general not effectively computable. The problem
can be solved in two ways:
• In verification, the end user must provide the inductive property
(chapters 25 and 26). Unless the properties are decidable, the verification that the given property is inductive cannot be fully automated and requires either user assistance for theorem provers or
even providing the proof whose validity is checked by proof assistants.
• For static analysis, the strongest inductive property will be approximated by abstraction (chapter 27) and extrapolation/interpolation
(chapter 34) techniques, which yield an effective but incomplete solution.
Because static analyzers must infer an inductive property that is provided
to verifiers, and this inductive property might need to be the exact abstraction of the collecting semantics, sound static analysis is more difficult than
882

sound verification, at least for infinite abstract domains (not reducible to
finite ones) [277].

52.3

Completeness by Calculational Design

Completeness of formal verification or static analysis methods states that
if a program property holds for all program executions as defined by the
program semantics, then the formal method can always be used to prove
it. Completeness comes in addition to a soundness requirement. In that
case, the calculational design will ensure soundness and completeness
whenever

.

Completeness is different from computability, and abstraction is not always a synonym for incompleteness. For example, verification methods
are often complete although, by Rice’s theorem 9.12, not fully automatizable (i.e. either the program property of interest cannot be expressed in
, or it can but the inductive proof is not fully mechanizable).
It is always possible to make an abstraction complete either by refining
to a more precise one (at the detriment of cost or computability) or by
abstracting to a coarser one (at the detriment of precision) [417]. The intuition is that the identity abstraction and the everywhere imprecise abstraction to tt are always complete. For example, [416] shows that for the
past and future temporal logic of [254], any abstraction is incomplete (except the identity and the everywhere imprecise ones). Otherwise stated,
any abstraction in that case must be imprecise unless it is a trivial one.

52.4
ness

Improving the Precision in Case of Incomplete-

By Rice theorem 9.12, incompleteness is unavoidable, for all programs.
This does not mean that for one program or one family of similar programs one cannot reach zero false alarms, as shown by Astrée for synchronous control command programs [113]. We can indefinitely refine
the abstraction, for example, by introducing new abstract domains in a
reduced product as in chapter 36 to cope with the origin of imprecision
or by refining the widening; see section 34.5. However, if the precision
increases the computation cost often increases disproportionately as the
class of considered program widens greatly. It is then necessary to ask
for user help or resort to other verification methods. Ultimately, the proof
must be done by hand, documented in the program, and redone after each
program or specification modification; see chapters 25 and 26 where the
expressiveness restrictions do not apply to manual proofs.
One possible user help is to select the abstract domains to be included in
the analyzer among a wide variety of abstract domains, each one adapted
883

to specific analysis objectives. This is possible for numerical domains but
the choice of symbolic domains is still limited at present.
Another possible form of user help is to add invariants to the program.
This often does not help when the invariant is overapproximated in the
analyzer’s abstract domains and the useful information provided by the
invariant is lost in its abstraction (e.g.„ a nonlinear invariant will be linearized). A solution is to express the invariants in a very expressive abstract domain known to the abstract interpreter and used only to reduce
the other abstract domains by user-provided invariants [397].

52.5

Handling Alarms

Soundness implies that all alarms be reported whether true or false. If
the analysis is too imprecise, the number of alarms may be very large.
Because true alarms require program correction, and the user does not
know which alarms are true of false, it may be important to propose an
order to deal with alarms. For example, in Astrée alarms resulting from
the undefinedness of the C semantics should be handled first (see the next
section 52.6). Some alarms may result from imprecisions already causing
previous alarms, so that a dependency analysis (chapter 47, e.g.„ [733]),
or more precisely a responsibility analysis [311] may be useful to handle
the original dominant alarms first [624]. True alarms may be identified
by abstract testing [995]. If only false alarms remain, the analysis must
ultimately be refined.

52.6

Handling Semantic Undefinedness

The entire issues of soundness and completeness rely on a formal definition of the language semantics. Many semantics leave some erroneous
program behaviors undefined. This does not prevent building sound verifiers and analyzers provided that the undefinedness is adequately reflected in the formal program semantics and explicitly reported to the
user.
A first issue is that the language semantics is not the one that is implemented (e.g.,. compilers have errors). A scientific approach is to prove
compilers correct [627] or to check the equivalence of the source and object code for each compiled program [833, 1003].
A second issue is that there might be no definition of the language semantics, either formal or informal. In that case, reasoning on program executions is reasoning on undefined objects, which is mathematical nonsense.
In that case, there is no way out, except by first defining the language
semantics. An example is [381] for Python.
Of course, the verification method or static analysis can be postulated,
884

which is therefore a definition of the semantics at an abstract level [376].
All mathematical theorems would be easier to prove if postulated in this
way. However, a correctness proof requires a program (a static analyzer
modeled by

, a specification

, and a proof that the program

semantics satisfies the specification that is

.

The third and most common issue is that the language has an informal
semantics from which a formal semantics can be derived but with imprecisions (e.g., some computations are undefined in the semantics when
something is going to happen anyway at runtime) [349, 466, 598, 757]. The
formal method is then sound if the expected result can be defined precisely whenever it may differ from the formal semantics. For example,
the formally undefined behaviors in C can be classified as follows [63]:
• An unspecified behavior occurs when several different behaviors are
allowed. If all possible behaviors can be taken into account, this is
a sound overapproximation. In practice this may be too imprecise,
so all possible behaviors cannot be taken into account. An underapproximation warning should be issued when some possible behaviors may not be taken into account.
An example is the order of execution of expressions, which may vary
for each use. A solution is, for example, a determinacy analysis ensuring that all evaluation orders are equivalent, and issuing a warning otherwise. Another solution is to use a parameter specifying
which compiler is to be used and analyzing the expression in the
order of the code generated by that compiler, if available.
• An implementation defined behavior1 is an unspecified behavior, but
the compiler has to document its choice.
For example, the size and endianness of integers. This can be handled by parameterizing the analysis. Another example is signed integer overflow, which the compiler may handle as modulo arithmetic
or as an error (a sound analysis will signal the potential error and,
depending on what might happen at execution [319], e.g., go on with
any integer value).
• For undefined behaviors, the C standard imposes no requirements at
all.
For example, the program can crash after dereferencing a NULL or
dangling pointer or after sequent point violation (modifying a memory location more than once between two sequence points).
A sound approach is to signal all undefined behaviors, go on with
correct behaviors, with the explicit warning that the analysis is no
longer valid after such an error if it ever happens at runtime. Other-

885

wise stated, the semantics defines the maximal executions up to the
first undefined behavior, if any, and the analysis is sound for that
semantics. Any execution that possibly differs from this semantics
must be statically reported.
Handling semantic undefinedness is always possible in a sound way by
defining exactly when undefined behaviors may occur in the semantics
P
{undefined behaviors}. In case of overapproximation, an error may not always occur at a program point. A solution is to continue
the analysis from that program point in the cases when the error with
undefined behavior does not occur. This is an underapproximation in
but all subsequent warnings by the analyzer are still potentially possible (unless it is a false alarm). If the error with undefined behavior does
not occur at runtime (e.g., it was a false alarm), the analysis based on
the formal semantics coincides with the runtime execution. Otherwise,
if the error with undefined behavior does occur at runtime (it was a true
alarm), the results of the analysis coincide with the runtime executions up
to the point where the first undefined behavior does appear at runtime.
No conclusion of the analysis on the runtime executions is valid after the
occurrence of the error. It follows that static analysis warnings relative
to semantic undefinedness should be considered first. When eliminated
by program rewriting or correction, or refinement of the static analyzer,
the semantics and runtime executions coincide exactly.
This is the point of view taken by typing in chapter 49 where the semantics
makes clear which runtime errors are captured by types (which we called
static errors) and those that are not (which we called dynamic errors).
Similarly, the soundness of Astrée is precisely defined and reported to
the user. Another example is [183] for Clousot [360].

52.7

Handling Missing Code

In many applications, the code calls libraries, for which the source, often
written in another language, is not available. If the library or operating
system is well documented, it is possible to write stubs that given an abstract precondition return a abstract postcondition that is valid after a
library/system call [765]. In absence of documentation, the only sound solution is to return “top/everywhere undefined,” which typically will propagate everywhere and produce many false alarms. An intermediate solution is to ask the programmer for a hypothesis after the call. In that case,
soundness is obviously relative to the veracity of this hypothesis. This is
the solution adopted in Astrée where, for example, end users have to provide intervals of values for inputs. A good practice is to provide larger
intervals than necessary to prove the robustness of the code.

886

52.8

Unsoundness

Commercial sound static analyzers are an order of magnitude harder and
costly to design [148] and hence much more expensive than unsound ones.
Soundness is hard to sell because it is not certain that end users and their
managers and even scientists [638] understand perfectly what soundness
means and its benefit when they choose a static analysis tool. So, many
commercial analyzers adopt easy and inexpensive unsound solutions.
52.8.1

Omitting and Hiding Alarms

Unsound analyzers often produce many more alarms than sound ones
(while missing many other ones). Nevertheless they are often popular
with unscrupulous programmers because unsound analyzers hide most
alarms, showing only those considered the most probable according to
some heuristic.
A sound solution, implemented in Polyspace Code Prover [317, 350], is to
distinguish between no error (green in Polyspace Code Prover), definite
error (red), or potential error (gray in Polyspace Code Prover). Eliminating definite errors first usually also eliminates false alarms in potential
errors. More generally, rather than hiding potential but not definite errors, while omitting some definite errors, it is better to be sound and to
help the end user in dealing with alarms. Solutions include exhibiting
an order in which definite/potential errors should be handled, for example, [624], and refining the analysis, for example, chapter 51 to ultimately
prove correctness or propose a counterexample, for example, [994, 995].
52.8.2

Bounding Execution

Some programs have a bounded execution. It is then sound to take this
bound on executions into account. For example, in control-command of
an airplane in which a loop is executed every 5 ms and the plane has,
because of physical limitations, a maximum flight time of 10 hours (for
instance 20 hours by precaution), it is safe to limit the number of iterations of the loop to 20 h/5 ms = 14,400,000. However, if the program is
not reinitialized at each stop of the plane, the static analysis with this
hypothesis would be unsound beyond 20 hours. For the same reason,
unrolling the loop n times less than 14,400,000 times is unsound [119].
So, comparing the precision and performances of n times loop unrolling
with bounded execution with widening is unfair [725] without considering soundness and scalaility, because the soundly checked specifications
are different, unless n 14,400,000, which is unlikely for a large nontrivial control-command program.

887

52.8.3

Unsoundiness

Many commercial static analyzers are unsound, in a way that is nowhere
defined, and their creators remain silent about unsoundness [182]. Of
course, truthiness would be easier for charlatans who would not feel the
need to tell the truth, including by omission, a situation not so uncommon,
even in some scientific circles.
However, this approach is rejected, with very few exceptions, by most
scientists who are not ready to abandon mathematical rigor whenever
applicable. Abstract interpretation obviously shows that mathematical
rigor is, of course, applicable in program verification and analysis.
Unsound methods provide no guarantee and so are essentially debugging
tools [114]. Because the debugging is not carried on executions, it is imprecise. Unsound analyses may go on forever, always reporting new bugs,
real or imaginary. Unsound analyzers may change the reporting diagnostics, including regressions that no longer report some bugs, after any release of a new version of the tool [114]. In summary, there is no notion of
scientific progress without soundness.
Verifiers and static analyzers are programs that can have bugs. Nevertheless, they can and should be proved to satisfy the specification provided
by the abstract semantics. Notice that for static analyzers the correctness
of inductive property inference need not be checked. Only the inductiveness check must be proved sound (and could be a separate tool extracted
from the soundness proof of the abstract semantics).
Of course, even if everything is proved correct, the compiler, operating
system, machine, verifier, and static analyzer may have, and will have,
bugs. This is not a serious enough pretext to abandon rigor. Mathematicians also produce wrong proofs. This does not prevent them from trying
to correct the errors in their proofs or redesign correct ones. At least the
formal methods offer a systematic approach to converge toward correct
verification or inference of trustworthy program properties.

52.9

Formal Development of Static Analyzers

The advantage of a formal soundness basis for a static analyzer is that
it can be constructed by calculational design. Presently this is mainly a
guideline for informal design, or an posteriori check of correctness [161,
546]. This paves the way for the design of tools based on algebraic manipulations that could perform the symbolic calculations automatically, as
is already the case in computer algebra systems, for example, maple for
integration [655].

888

52.10

Conclusion

Abstract interpretation provides a formal approach to the design of semantics, and program verification and analysis methods. The soundness
condition is the basis for the calculational design of these formal methods.
Already, metatools can be used to check this calculational design [93, 126,
127, 546]. Beyond post-design verification, calculational design assistants
will hopefully be built to assist, and hopefully automatize, this formal calculational design.
1. 1 There are also locale-specific behaviors that can be handled as the
implementation-defined behaviors.

53
Static Analysis Tools
We quickly review and categorize the broad spectrum of static software
analysis tools and the resources available or needed to build these tools.
We consider only automatic tools that require only lightweight specifications (such as machine parameterization or assertions to be checked), do
not run the code, and need no user intervention to support the analysis.
Contents
53.1

A Broad Spectrum of Static Analysis Tools

53.2

On the Design of Static Analyzers

53.3

Beyond Program Static Analysis

53.4

Conclusion and Perspectives

53.1

A Broad Spectrum of Static Analysis Tools

Compilers (such as CLang [620]) are widely used in the software development cycle. They provide selected elementary definite errors and potential warnings. Compilers with advanced type checking or inference such
as Ocaml are useful to eliminate careless mistakes such as nonmatching
formal parameters and actual arguments. Every programmer benefits
from such tools.
A second level of static analysis tools is linters. The Unix Lint command
[534] was one of the first widely available static analyzers to report
errors such as unused variables and functions, use before initialization,
unreachable code, unused returned values of functions, type checking
889

(more precise than the C compiler at the time), nonportable features,
pointer misalignments, and other errors. Bugs are found mostly by
pattern matching but may use more sophisticated data flow analyses.
Some code analyzers (such as Microsoft’s Roslyn or LGTM from Semmle)
are extensible and allow for defining programming style rules for code
quality. This is useful mainly for junior programmers to help them think
about basic potential problems in their code.
A third level is that of wide-scope, almost always unsound and commercial, static analysis tools. They target a wide range of programming
languages, development environments, and deployment platforms. It
is therefore difficult to take semantic specificities into account. For
example, Coverity [350] “supports 21 languages and over 70 frameworks
and templates” in 2021. One emphasis is speed, often based on unsound
techniques. For example, [182] mentioned that Coverity analyze loops by
considering the very first few iterations only. Software models checkers
such as CBMC unroll loops a bounded number of times, so belong to
this category of unsound static analyzers. Another emphasis is the
user interface, filtering out less frequent errors at first, providing error
explanations, and correction suggestions. This explains why professional
programmers enjoy these tools. Empirically based, such bug-finders help
but provide no guarantee at all, and so are inadequate for certification.
At the fourth level, static analysis tools are semantics based, sound, and
precise. Based on a sound abstraction of the program semantics properties, they need to automatically do mathematical inference. They never
miss any error in the well defined category of bugs that they consider
(e.g., runtime errors) under well defined and checked hypotheses on runtime behavior hypotheses (e.g., undefined behaviors in C). They require
parameterization to specify semantic parameters (such as word size, endianness, etc.). For industrial codes of millions of lines, the analysis time
can be minutes to hours. So the objective is not immediate interactive
support. They are useful for highly qualified engineers looking for the
highest level of robustness, safety, and security. An example is Astrée,
originally designed for embedded control-command. When applied to
domain-specific applications, they provide no false alarm ([307, 696, 904]).
When extended outside their original domain of specialization (e.g., large
ARINC 653 and POSIX multithreaded applications for Astrée[696]), they
remain precise enough not to be overwhelming.
Of course, this categorization only points out a few tool characteristics
in a very large spectrum of formal or informal foundations, scope of analyzed properties, analysis cost and precision, ease of use, intended application domain, and targeted academic or industrial public [269]. Most
static analysis tools have characteristics of all categories and so are very
hard to evaluate objectively and precisely, in particular for soundness.
Examples are C Global Surveyor [955] and IKOS[145] developed by Guil890

laume Brat and Arnaud Venet for the NASA Mars missions; Kestrel Technology CodeHawk[196]; CodeSonar from GrammaTech; Polyspace Code
Proveroriginally developed by Alain Deutsch; Sparroworiginally developed at the Seoul National University [485]; and others.

53.2

On the Design of Static Analyzers

53.2.1

Specifications

Formal language semantics specifications and software developing
guidelines should be the reference for building static analyzers. They
are mostly missing. Exceptions are MISRA C for the automotive industry
[63] and DO-178C for the avionics industry, among others (ISO 26262, IEC
61508, EN 50128, etc.). If syntactic rules are trivial to check, precise and
scalable static analysis is indispensable to check for undecidable rules
(e.g.„ rulechecker of AbsInt).
53.2.2

Certification

Sound static analyzers provide a guarantee on the final result of a software development. They are also very useful during the development
phase for early bug detection. Unfortunately, software certification is often optional and more an obligation of means during development rather
than an obligation of results on the product. The use of static analyzers,
even incorrect ones, is therefore a facility rather than an obligation.
53.2.3

Benchmarks

Benchmarks are indispensable during the design of static analyzers to
adapt the analysis to the application domain. Most available benchmarks
are for academic tools and do not reflect at all the difficulties encountered
in industrial code. This is made clear, for example, by [977], showing the
limits of academic tools working very well on tailored academic benchmarks but failing on industrial code, even very small ones. Obviously,
industrial benchmarks should be made available publicly, for example,
[821] or, at least, to tool design and evaluation teams.
53.2.4

Control Architecture

There are essentially two types of static analyzers. The vast majority
are based on an intermediate language targeting multiple languages
(e.g., Clousot [360] for the .NET framework languages compiling to
the common intermediate language (CIL)). Very few use the structural
approach propounded in this book (e.g., Astréeand Zoncolan, developed

891

by Francesco Logozzo and Manuel Fähndrich at Facebook for scalable
information-flow analysis with application to security and privacy [334]).
The frontend, similar to that of a compiler, is the easiest and most wellunderstood part of a static analyzer. Hence the effort saved by considering an intermediate language is insignificant compared with the many
difficulties they generate (e.g., to report at the source level, to take the
program structure and the language specificities into account, etc.). Moreover, if information in the intermediate language is needed, it can be easily added to the program representation.
The control architecture is essential for determining inductive invariant
for mathematical induction (by widening and narrowing and their duals). In more complex situations, the structure on which induction is performed may have to be determined during the analysis itself (see, for example, the segmentation concept in [263]).
53.2.5

Property Architecture

Another basic early decision to be taken in the design of static analyzers is
how abstract properties will be represented and implemented. We have
chosen to use abstract domains combined with functors like the reduced
product, as in Astrée. This decomposes a difficult problem into subproblems that are easier to master. A counterexample is Infer in which properties are represented by logical formulas and operations like widening
are left implicit and distributed all over the code. A restructuration is
apparent in the publicly available code but the kernel is left inextricable.
53.2.6

Extensibility

Because it is very hard to predict which specific inductive properties will
be ultimately necessary to cope with specified errors, it is absolutely essential that the property architecture be extensible in a structured way.
This is the whole purpose of the abstract domains and the domain functors/combinators. Plug-ins such as Eva plug-in [155] can be used to implement new abstract domains in the static analyzer of the Frama-C [282,
579] source-code analyzer and verifier. It is harder to influence their
combinations. Astréewas designed right at the beginning for extensibility
[267].
53.2.7

Scalability

Analyzers that do not scale may still be useful to analyze small program
parts. They may be used on purely functional modular software. However, most industrial software is not decomposable into small modular
functional units. Those programs usually have millions of lines sharing
892

a complex global state. Then scalability becomes a central problem [70].
Scalability must be thought about right at the beginning of the static analyzer design. For example, Astréedoes not use a reduced product but a
complex rather efficient overapproximation of the reduced product [268].
It’s industrial version by AbsInt scales to tens of millions of lines of C with
high precision.
53.2.8

Libraries

Abstract domain libraries such as APRON [529],
[897], or PPL [69,
98, 99] for numerical properties are extremely useful both to spread
know-how and to be used in different analyzers. Unfortunately, symbolic
properties are much harder to formalize independently of particular
languages, and no largely distributed library is available.
53.2.9

Generators

Static analyzer generators, similar to compiler-compilers or compiler generators and going beyond parser generators, might be useful at least for
rapid prototyping [980]. An early example is PAG, a generic abstract interpreter covering chapters 21, 23, 28, and 45 [661, 662]. However the
technology has not matured enough to be used in most compiler or static
analyzer projects. Crabis an analyzer of a programming language independent intermediate language [744]. The SPARTA library provides the
basic blocks for building static analyzers based on Abstract Interpretation
[905].
53.2.10

Qualification

There are very few requirements on the static analysis tools used in industry. An exception is the DO-333 [377] supplement to DO-178C, providing
guidance on the processes necessary to qualify a tool that will be used to
claim DO-178C objectives. One must show that if the program has a bug in
the category considered by the tool, it must be signaled. So, an unsound
static analyzer cannot be qualified (but an imprecise one can). Moreover,
signaled bugs must be handled according to the procedures defined by the
DO-178C (so an imprecise analyzer will require much more extra work).
Astréeis DO-333 qualified, thus saving a lot of redundant testing work.
53.2.11

Library Verification

Some libraries are known to be erroneous (such as APRON’s not reporting
float overflows or nonterminating on the polyhedra domain because of
rounding errors. Rationals should be used but are expensive because the
denominators tend to be very large. This is the reason why polyhedra are
893

not used in Astrée). A few abstract domain libraries have been formally
verified, such as octagons [544]. It is also possible to check the result of
each analysis, a posteriori, after the program analysis [101, 379].
53.2.12

Static Analyzer Verification

The computer-aided verification of static analyzers would go much beyond qualification and ideally would help in the calculational design propounded in this book. Verasco[544, 546] is an example of academic static
analyzer verified using the proof assistant COQ [520]. An analyzer like
Astréeis about 265,000 lines of OCaml (not counting the much larger user
interface) in 2021, so that a formal verification is not in the reach of proof
checkers or theorem provers at that time.
53.2.13

Evaluation and Benchmarking

Evaluations of the soundness, precision, and scalability of static analyzers by independent authorities are extremely rare, leaving place for academic fantasies or grandiloquent commercial arguments. An exception
is [122], in which only Astréeand Frama-C Eva plug-in were found sound
(and even detected unexpected errors in the test set) and precise enough
to fully handle all alarms. Analyzers that failed are not reported, although
this would be important information. The license of some commercial
analyzers even forbids making evaluations public. More honest peer reviews like [122, 493, 977, 982] are necessary to guide research in fruitful
directions and orient credulous users in their difficult tool choice. Such
work is useful but often difficult to publish.
53.2.14

Industrialization

The industrialization of a static analyzer, most often with an academic origin, is a difficult task going much beyond what the academic world can
produce. The adaptation to special needs and standards, the documentation, the user interface, and other essentials most often requires more
work that the analyzer itself. This can hardly be done outside an industrial context. This too often means compromises with rigor. But there are
exceptions, such as AbsInt (www.absint.com).
53.2.15

Human Resources

The design of a static analyzer is an order of magnitude more complicated
than that of a compiler. If elementary static analyzers (such as the programming project in the Project index) take a few days or weeks, academic projects a few months or years, an advanced static analyzer such
as Astréerequires decades of research and development.
894

Very few experienced highly qualified engineers can complete this task
with success. The successes often come after a strong academic background in the theory of program analysis and a large practical experience.
This hugely demanding combination is extremely rare, which might explain why very few scalable, sound, precise, perennial, and open sourced
or industrialized analyzers do exist.
53.2.16

Education

The adoption of static analysis in an industrial context requires that end
users understand the tool they are using. Most software engineers have a
fuzzy understanding of static analysis and could read [261, 837] as an introduction. A larger adoption would require a better education, for example, the use of static analyzers at the very beginning of programmers’ education, which beyond typing, which is a rather coarse analysis, is almost
never the case. Educational static analyzers are still missing, and educational licenses of professional static analyzers are underused.
53.2.17

Responsibility

Finally, the main obstacle to the wide adoption of static analyzers is that
programmers are never held responsible for their errors, even when the
human and economic consequences are huge. Contrary to other disciplines, software engineers are guaranteed qualified immunity under the
pretext that verification is beyond best practice. Rapid development with
user debugging and distant updates is the rule. If best practice included
the mandatory use of standards and qualified tools, programmers and
their hierarchy could be held accountable for bugs automatically discoverable by such tools, at least the definite ones. This would certainly encourage the community to use reliable tools and boost the static analysis
market [981].

53.3

Beyond Program Static Analysis

Beyond application to program analysis and verification, abstract interpretation has numerous other applications such as program development
[490]; controller synthesis [516]; program synthesis [962]; test generation
[548]; fuzz testing [851]; cellular signaling systems in biology [139, 140,
164, 367]; validation of the local robustness [44, 339, 407, 699, 893, 894]
and the absence of gender bias [939] of neural networks; machine learning [946]; verification of datadase query languages [527]; reactive systems
[290]; SMT solvers [284]; hybrid systems [458, 481]; Simulink [171] and
Lustre [454] models; games [483, 814]; energy consumption [356]; climate
models [826]; quantum computing [793, 997]; and others.

895

53.4

Conclusion and Perspectives

Although academic tools have severe limitations, some have scaled to an
industrial success, for example, for safety critical applications (too often
underadvertised due to severe confidentiality constraints and lack of independent comparative evaluations).
As programming languages and computer systems become more complex
and software as well as hardware much larger, a lot of problems remain
to be solved. For example, the analysis of complex data structures; of
hardware and their memory models; of concurrency; of operating systems [178]; of distributed, real-time, and hybrid systems are still in their
infancy.
Moreover, program analysis must be broaden to systems analysis of a program together with a model of the environment with which the program
interacts. A challenging example is closing the loop in cyber physical systems (instead of analyzing the program under input-output hypotheses),
for example, to prove stability and robustness [229]. Another challenging
example would be to analyze the code of a social network to prove that it
correctly implements the officially published privacy policy.
Finally, by undecidability, soundness, precision, and scalability will remain an interesting challenge, forever.

54.1

On the Scope of Abstract Interpretation

Verification methods (including model checking) and static analysis methods are the subject of tens of thousands of publications (e.g.„ internet
search engines of “static program analysis” produce millions of results).
Abstract interpretation provides a unified understanding of this literature
as well as intellectual tools to go far beyond the present-day state of the
art. Following [713, p. 1],
“We lay down a fundamental principle of generalization by abstraction: The
existence of analogies between central features of various theories implies
the existence of a general theory which underlies the particular theories
and unifies them with respect to those central features.”
More than a disparate collection of unrelated techniques and algorithms
(e.g.„ [191]), abstract interpretation offers a uniform abstract mathematical framework to understand formal methods and to design the
semantics, specifications, proof methods, data flow analysis, model
checking, typing, static analysis, and other components of computer
systems described by a formal language. The abstract interpretation
theory is generic, general, uniform, and practically applicable to any
system evolving in time (see a few nonconventional examples in section
53.3). It is an effective method for constructing sound-by-construction
formal methods and tools.

54.2

Principles of Abstract Interpretation

Abstract interpretation is a mathematical theory of exact or approximate abstraction. We have introduced the theoretical foundations and
provided several examples of application to the semantics, verification
and static analysis of programming languages. Hopefully, this book will
broaden the understanding of what it means to reason on programs and
to reason on methods to reason on and manipulate programs.
The principle of abstraction that we have used recurrently in all chapters
is the following.
• Let ℘( ),
be properties of entities (the so-called concrete domain)
that we want to prove for a given entity of ;
• Consider a subset
℘( ) of properties of interest , ;

897

• Encode these properties of interest in an abstract domain A, ;
• The decoding function γ A
is called the concretization function;
• Make proofs and analyses using abstract properties only;
• So, because the expressivity is limited to = γ(A), any concrete property in ℘( ) must be overapproximated (or dually underapproximated) by an abstract property in A;
• If the abstract proof/analysis succeeds, it is valid in the concrete
(soundness);
• If all such proofs can always be done in the abstract, the approach
is complete because no approximation is ever necessary; and
• If the abstract proof/exact analysis may sometime fail, some properties in ℘( ) that are essential in the concrete proof are missed in
the abstract (incompleteness).
In case every concrete property has a best abstraction, we have a Galois
connection

(chapter 11).

We have rigorously followed this approach for program semantics, verification, and static analysis. The same abstraction principle can be applied
to A, , which yields a hierarchy of abstractions.

54.3

Semantics

For semantics, we postulated a prefix stateless trace semantics in chapter
6 that is equivalent to the maximal trace semantics of chapter 7 (equivalent in the sense that each one is an abstraction of the other). This level
of abstraction was appropriate for all the applications we considered (including recovering by abstraction of a classic stateful trace semantics in
chapter 42).
Were semantics not precise enough, we would have had to propose a refinement and show that the prefix trace semantics is an abstraction of this
refinement. This would ensure, by composition of abstractions, that the
rest of the book would be consistent with this refined semantics.
For some applications, the prefix trace semantics is too refined. So, we
considered several more abstract semantics for invariance/reachability
in chapter 19, invariance verification conditions in chapter 25, Hoare
logic in chapter 26, Cartesian invariants in chapter 28, stateful prefix
traces in chapter 42, and transition systems in chapter 43.
All semantics are presented inductively, in structural form (by induction
on the program syntax of chapter 4), and using equivalently either deductive definitions or fixpoint definitions (chapter 15). The advantage is
that we can use inductive proofs everywhere, which is indispensable to
reason on infinite objects (chapter 16). Moreover, by observing that abstractions are relating abstract domains we were able to show in chapter
898

21 that all semantics have a similar structure formalized by an abstract interpreter and differ only by the abstract domain taken in parameter. This
greatly simplifies soundness proofs that must be done for each particular
abstract domain but only once for the abstract interpreter (chapter 27).
Moreover, it paves the way for calculational design and hopefully, in the
future, of computer-aided design of formal methods. This provides strong
design guidelines and ensures correctness by construction [322, 324, 327]
as opposed to posteriori verification [501, 504]. The abstract interpreter
can itself be the subject of abstract interpretation [278], for example, to
perform induction during static analysis.

54.4

Verification

Verification methods in chapters 25 and 26 are derived from abstract semantics by applying structural, fixpoint, or iteration induction studied in
chapter 24. They can themselves, when parameterized by an abstract domain, be expressed as abstract semantics.

54.5

Static Analysis

Static analysis aims at automation of verification methods. Because of
Rice’s theorem in chapter 9, a static analysis method is always in one of
the following categories.
• 1. unsound;
• 2. sound and potentially nonterminating (or getting out of resources) as illustrated in chapter 44;
• 3. sound, terminating, and potentially producing false alarms (in all
other static analysis chapters).
Abstract interpretation theorizes the last two possibilities (the first empirical and too frequent alternative needing no theory at all because nothing
is ever guaranteed).
The main criticisms are that abstract interpretation does not provide
a definite method to design useful abstractions and that abstract
interpretation-based static analyzers have false alarms.
__ The same way that mathematics does not provide the proof of your
theorem but tools to help you make the proof, the theory of abstract interpretation does not provide the abstraction to design your static analyzer
but tools to help you design your abstraction (such as reduction and the
reduced product in chapters 29 and 36). Coming up with the right abstraction providing the best cost/precision ratio is almost never easy. It
is presently an art supported by a purely experimental science. This was
made clear by the evolutionary design of Astréeor, for example, [974].

899

__ By Rice’s theorem, any completely automatic analysis method is
doomed to fail on infinitely many programs. For example, decidable
methods apply only to restricted classes of programs that do not fit well
to practice. When not applicable, the only sound conclusion is that
everything is an alarm. One can also argue that computers are finite,
so undecidability can be bypassed. But then combinatorial explosion
strikes on infinitely many programs. Running out of resources is even
worse that false alarms.
Static analysis has been defined by abstraction (chapter 27) presented
structurally, and, in absence of a general method to compute direct solutions of fixpoint equations, by iterative fixpoint computation (chapter
15) or approximation (chapter 34) and checking (chapter 35), reducing
various iteration strategies to chaotic iterations (chapter 22).
So, the main challenge is to study abstractions well suited for specific program properties and to combine them astutely to achieve enough precision at reasonable cost. It is a matter of both theoretical studies and experimentation. As we say in French, « À l’impossible nul n’est tenu ».
The examples we have considered are both Cartesian and relational, history sensitive and flow sensitive and insensitive, numerical and symbolic,
complete and incomplete, monotrace based and multitrace based, all of
them being sound.
Exercise 54.1 Categorize the various verification methods and static analyses provided in the book according to the preceding classification.

54.6

The Future of Abstract Interpretation

Abstract interpretation has shown itself to be a transversal idea applicable to a large variety of formal methods and to scale to industrial practice.
Much more is certainly to come!
The future of abstract interpretation is in the hand of talented generations of researchers and engineers who master all necessary intricacies
of the theory and practice. This book is a first step in that direction to be
complemented by a study of the literature.
Hopefully, the readers will take up abstract interpretation and successfully design new abstractions, methods, and tools, and extend its application domains.
